items.content:
Triangle InfoSeCon Panel Recap: How Security Leaders Prove Defenses, Respond to Breaches and Recover
By:
Amanda Kegley
November 5, 2026
Prove your controls continuously, know where your sensitive data lives and get to know your local FBI office before you need it: those were the lessons security leaders shared at Triangle InfoSeCon.
On Friday, October 30, 2026, I had the honor of moderating the leadership track panel
Raleigh ISSA’s annual security conference
. I was joined by three panelists: a CIO/CISO from a mid-sized clinical research organization, a field CISO and Trusted Advisor from Access IT Solutions (a Cymulate partner) and an FBI agent.
The discussion ranged from what boards ask for today to how AI agents are changing identity risk, why it’s important to establish a relationship with the FBI and why the hardest part of a breach often comes months after the incident is contained.
This blog summarizes the key lessons from that discussion with practical steps security teams can take now.
Key Takeaways
Layered security controls are essential
. Boards now ask for proof that layered security controls stop real attacks, not lists of tools or vanity metrics.
Attackers have evolved
. Attacks can now run from initial access to attempted exfiltration in about 24 hours, so testing, validation and training need to run continuously.
Be prepared for recovery post-incident
. Recovery is only as fast as your data inventory: classify, confine and delete sensitive data before an incident.
Establish a relationship with the FBI.
Reach out to your local FBI Field Office through
www.fbi.gov
to establish a relationship prior to an incident.
How has proving security posture to the board changed?
During the panel, I asked the room: How many of you are more than 95% confident that your security controls would stop an attack today, especially with AI in the mix? Not a single hand went up.
Every CISO gets the same question: "Are we secure?" (For more on
answering the board's "are we secure?" question
, see our earlier post.) A few years ago, board questions were simple and now they are more in-depth with evidence required.
Then
Now
What security products do we own?
Are we using those tools effectively?
How many phishing emails did we block?
How have our layered controls stopped real attacks?
What did the annual red team find?
How do we test ourselves continuously?
Are we keeping attackers out?
What could get out, and have we protected the right data?
Boards commonly ask for:
Real scenarios, not tool lists.
Walk the board through actual attacks and show how multi-layered protections stopped them.
An attack surface view.
Show evidence that you are continuously inventorying and reducing the attack surface, and
measuring cybersecurity posture
and threat resilience.
Data security posture.
Know where sensitive data lives and how it is protected, often with data security posture management (DSPM) tools.
Vanity metrics are disappearing.
Volume stats like "phishing emails blocked" told a simple story that no longer satisfies the board, especially as organizations adopt zero trust architectures and an assume-breach mindset, combined with how advanced attackers are with AI.
What gets out matters more than what gets in.
Smarter boards know incidents will happen. What they care about is what leaves the organization. Threat actors increasingly favor a smash-and-grab approach: instead of encrypting systems, they steal data and blackmail the victim. That is when the board asks the tough question: Where does our sensitive data live, and are we continuously validating that it is protected?
Point-in-time validation alone is no longer enough.
The traditional model was an annual red team test that produced findings, remediation and a roll-up into a risk register. Even an advanced SOC that collects alerts is still reacting. The panel’s view is that teams need continuous monitoring and validation to filter the noise, eliminate false positives and deliver board metrics in near real time.
No organization may be 95% confident, but security teams can replace confidence with continuous evidence of their threat resilience.
What are the biggest identity risks today, including AI agents?
Privileged accounts and standing privileges are the largest identity threat, for both human administrative accounts and AI agents.
Recommendation:
Move toward time-based, just-in-time access, where elevated privileges are granted for a limited window and then revoked. Apply this to AI agents and admin accounts alike.
Zero Trust is now practical.
Zero Trust architecture and tooling have matured significantly, with conditional access that includes device health checks and user-level risk controls, plus advanced logging and dashboards. More regulations now call for zero trust controls, which ties the architecture directly to governance and compliance.
AI agent risk is outpacing governance
Frameworks for securing AI are still maturing. NIST published the
AI Risk Management Framework
. In the meantime, the panel shared four steps organizations can take now:
Control the perimeter first.
A company deployed Cisco Umbrella after finding employees putting company data into personal ChatGPT accounts and using unapproved AI note-taking tools, including on customer calls. Now, the use of AI is fully monitored and controlled.
Limit what AI tools can ingest.
In Microsoft Copilot deployments, SharePoint sites can be open to Copilot ingestion by default, so anything someone shared globally can be crawled. That team turned this off everywhere and applied least privilege and least data.
Train people and publish an AI usage policy
so employees know what they can and can't do. This step is critical. Without a usage policy, employees will still find ways to use AI for day-to-day work, including entering business data into personal AI tools.
Trust, but verify.
The next area of security tooling is visibility into what data goes into AI tools and what agents do with it. Traditional software had test plans and requirements documents. AI needs equivalent testing harnesses and guardrails.
How fast are attackers moving now?
Attackers used to sit in an environment for months. Now attacks move much faster. In an example shared, the attack chain took about 24 hours from start to attempted data exfiltration, and it was automated end-to-end. Faster attacks leave less time to spot anomalies in your environment.
The skill barrier has dropped.
AI toolkits make social engineering far more convincing:
Phishing emails sent to finance teams look like real, overdue invoices.
Attacks arrive across Microsoft Teams channels, phone calls and text messages, including SMS messages impersonating the CEO and asking for money or gift cards.
As a general rule, if someone urgently requests something that isn't routine, stop and verify before acting. Years ago, an OPM investigator called me at 11 a.m. on a Saturday. It turned out to be legitimate when I called back during the workweek, but that habit of pausing has saved me from many scams, from fake bank alerts to online shopping sites. I won't buy from an online store unless I know the seller or have checked that its domain is legitimate. I also signed up for the
Federal Trade Commission consumer alerts
, which I encourage everyone to do.
Living off the land still works.
Once an attacker is inside, east-west movement is often unchecked. Fully segmenting a network or hosts takes significant effort, and usable tooling to stop lateral movement is still limited. Continuous validation of segmentation controls with proof attackers are stopped is essential.
The patch wave is a board topic.
Boards are asking whether the current volume of security patches will continue. One panelist called this an inflection point: decades of software were written without tools that could scan for these flaws, and AI-driven scanning is now surfacing them quickly. The hope is that the volume levels off over the next year and leaves more secure software behind, but only time will tell.
Training has to move at attack speed.
Periodic, generic security training is outdated by the time it arrives. A company’s CISO now uses an AI tool to turn a short script into a five-minute video. When a new lure appears in the morning, employees have a training video by mid-afternoon, with real examples of SMS, CAPTCHA and Teams-based attacks. Hearing from peer CISOs about what they are seeing helps teams build these trainings even faster.
This shift is also happening at the national level. Earlier this year, the White House invited industry in, for the first time, to share how defenders can respond at machine speed as attackers move at machine speed. The administration is working to remove barriers, engage industry more and prototype faster. Read
my recap of the White House AI cyber defense roundtable
to learn more.
How often should you test your defenses?
Testing your controls once a year doesn’t work. The right cadence depends on moving from reactive alerting to active, continuous monitoring. The panel shared two practical lessons.
Rotate perspectives.
Threat actors probe your perimeter in many different ways. Switching penetration testing vendors, or adding more than one, brings fresh perspectives on your external attack surface, even at extra cost. And don't stop at validating where attackers can get in: test how far they can move and how much damage they can cause once they're in.
Continuously test and validate every layer.
I always assume the attacker is already in, which is the premise of Zero Trust: assume breach.
Breach and attack simulation
, which has evolved into exposure validation, has moved from a nice-to-have to a must-have for continuous validation. More organizations now treat it as an operational cyber capability their security teams use daily. Agentic AI has removed the need for specialized skills and answers common questions such as "Which attacks should I run, and how often?" It knows your environment, identifies threats relevant to you and runs the attacks automatically. For example, with two-way integrations with your SIEM and EDR, it can identify a new threat in your environment, reveal a missed detection, automatically push the IOC and vendor-specific detection rule in your tools, and then re-test to verify the fix. At Cymulate, this is what we call
agentic cyber defense engineering
.
What do you need ready before an incident?
When I asked the audience of CISOs and security leaders how many of them had run a ransomware tabletop exercise in the past 12 months, about half raised their hands, which shows this is still an area to work on. One panelist shared how he learned this the hard way. When his first incident hit, he had just started the job. He didn't know who the cyber insurance provider was, and the incident response plan had no detailed instructions and hadn't been updated in years.
Tabletop exercises help, but the panel recommended building a comprehensive named contact list in advance with processes:
Cyber insurance provider
External counsel
Forensics firm
to determine whether attackers are still in your systems
Negotiator
to buy time, get proof of life and confirm what the attackers actually have
A data inventory capability
so you know what was taken (more on this below)
Local FBI Office
The FBI agent panelist encourages companies to establish a relationship with their local
FBI
office.  Check out their website for their
FBI cyber services
.
Should you pay the ransom?
Boards ask this question constantly, and that panelist's answer has stayed the same: don't pay.
Money keeps threat actors going.
Not paying is more painful in the short term, but it takes the oxygen out of the room.
Fewer organizations are paying.
So much data is already exposed that paying to keep it private often means little; the stolen data likely circulates either way.
You'll likely notify customers anyway.
After one incident, he had to talk to hundreds of customers about exposed data, and he would have had to notify them even if the data hadn't been released.
Another panelist shared a cautionary example. Around a merger, a U.S. company had paid a ransom in bitcoin twice. After the acquisition was announced, the same attackers used living-off-the-land techniques to move into the parent company. They were caught by checking backups, which had been tampered with, and stopped a day or two before encryption. Multiple layers of backups, including tape, saved the business. The lesson: paying didn't make the problem go away.
Prepare for escalation beyond the network
Extortion now reaches into the physical world. A panelist described a case of executive swatting, where threat actors called in false emergencies to an executive’s home, and the organization had to work with local police as a result. Plan for this before an incident, not during one.
Why does post-breach recovery take so long?
Getting systems back up is only part of recovery. Four months after a single incident, one panelist's team was still notifying customers, because they had to work through massive SharePoint sites to determine what had bee taken and kept learning more about the damage to customer data.
Data inventory is the hardest post-breach task
Looking back, if the organization had a DSPM tool in place, it could have known in minutes which customers were affected and what type of data was involved, such as sensitive patient data or contract data, based on data tagging. These are Zero Trust best practices for the data pillar.
In my experience, data has historically been the least mature pillar of Zero Trust architecture, but that is changing. Even at the White House event, data challenges came up consistently during open discussions.
Data retention policy determines blast radius
One panelist said his organization's retention policy had effectively been "we never get rid of anything." With a background as a chief data and AI officer, his mindset had always been that more data is good. But now that attackers focus on smash-and-grab, sensitive data is also a major liability. "Blast radius" is a term he uses with the board all the time.
Best practices from the panel:
Classify and tag data,
especially unstructured data moving through email and collaboration tools, and carry tags into other platforms.
Protect the crown jewels
with tight controls, and continuously validate protection and detection.
Cold-archive or delete
what you don't need.
Confine sensitive data
to a small number of tightly controlled areas. At that panelist's organization, sensitive data had spread across every SharePoint site. After cleanup, it now lives only in a few controlled locations.
As AI and agents make it easier for data to flow out the door, data protection measures such as tagging and classification matter more than ever.
How is red teaming evolving?
Red teaming is moving beyond point-in-time testing. One panelist described a test where the red team couldn't get in from the outside, so his team deliberately opened a path and let them in to see whether they could detect lateral movement. That revealed living-off-the-land activity and where else an attacker could go. Teams need to be flexible about where the red team starts, and use
automated red teaming
to schedule ongoing tests that validate prevention and detection and monitor for drift.
Many generic attacks also don't reflect your actual environment. The panel expects AI-driven red teaming to become:
Hyper-personalized:
profiling your environment, knowing who is targeting you and focusing on attack sequences that reach your most sensitive data stores.
Prioritized:
accounting for compensating controls that may already cover a vulnerability before it is patched.
Closed-loop:
pushing the fix and re-verifying it automatically, which answers the common question of how often attacks should run.
The
MITRE ATT&CK framework
is evolving as well. MITRE is releasing protection strategies down to the configuration level, such as checking whether MFA is disabled in Microsoft 365 (
MITRE ATT&CK
). Because Zero Trust is policy-driven, an adversary who gets in can turn off a conditional access policy, so configuration drift monitoring matters: MFA can be on one day and off the next. MITRE has opened a Slack channel for the community to contribute feedback. Learn more in my
recent blog on the protection strategy structure and how to engage MITRE
.
Key takeaways from the panel
Security is everyone's responsibility,
and it starts with leadership.
Use the momentum after an incident.
Budget often opens up right after an attack for the platform you were told to wait on, such as a Zero Trust architecture. Bring teams together, run a good lessons-learned review and document where your weaknesses are.
Run retrospectives and keep training current.
After an incident, review what happened and turn real attacker lures into fast, specific training.
Don't let urgency override judgment.
Any message that demands payment right now is a red flag. Stop and verify, because legitimate requests rarely work that way.
Verify domains before you trust them.
Check WHOIS for when a domain was registered, at work and in your personal life. A domain that appeared yesterday claiming they have been in business for awhile is a strong warning sign.
Security doesn't stop at work.
Apply these lessons to your personal life to protect yourself, such as the earlier recommendation to sign up for FBI cyber alerts.
How Cymulate helps prove controls work across the incident lifecycle
Many of the panel's lessons come back to one need: evidence of security controls and measured threat resilience. Boards want proof that layered controls stop real attacks, security teams need to know what an attacker can reach after initial access, and both need answers continuously, not once a year.
Prove.
Cymulate Exposure Validation
runs safe, automated attack scenarios against your production controls, including assume-breach lateral movement, living-off-the-land techniques and data exfiltration, so you can show which layers prevent and detect real attacker behavior.
Prioritize.
Cymulate CTEM
moves beyond exposure discovery to prove exploitability and prioritize based on business impact, accounting for compensating controls and giving the board outcome-based evidence instead of activity counts.
Adapt.
The
Cymulate Platform
delivers vendor-specific mitigations for identified gaps, including detection rules and IoCs and re-testing verifies each fix. With
Cymulate Cowork
, powered by Vero AI, AI agents automate repeatable exposure validation workflows so security teams can keep pace with attacks that now unfold in hours.
Ready to prove your defenses before the next incident?
The organizations best prepared for a breach are the ones that test their assumptions before an attacker does. To see how Cymulate provides continuous evidence that your controls work,
schedule a demo
.
Amanda Kegley
Amanda Kegley has over 15 years of experience in cybersecurity. With her in-depth knowledge of security needs in today’s dynamic threat landscape, she successfully innovates and markets new cybersecurity capabilities.

items.content:
通往 root 的路径，减少一千条 | OpenAI
2026年11月4日
安全
刊发
通往 root 的路径，减少一千条
我们开发了一条自主完成漏洞发现、利用和修补的流水线。在使用我们的网络安全模型进行的一次运行中，它验证了 Linux 中的 948 个本地权限提升漏洞并生成了补丁，API 成本为 120 万美元。
聆听文章
31:33
分享
过去，安全研究需要对每个发现的问题单独开展持续调查；如今，这项工作正日益能够作为系统化流程来执行。本文介绍了我们在这一领域的一项探索。
漏洞发现正变得更容易规模化，但优先级判定和验证仍是实际工作中的瓶颈。我们构建了一个原型，在受控的研究环境中查找 Linux 内核中的安全缺陷。该原型识别并分析了 2,308 个疑似 Linux 内核漏洞，动态复现了 1,724 个漏洞，并生成了 948 个本地权限提升（LPE）利用程序，可使无特权的本地用户获得 root 权限。
我们根据这些证据确定漏洞报告的优先级，并开发了候选补丁供维护者审核。按照 Linux 内核社区的指导，我们从关键漏洞入手，并正与 Patch the Planet 合作伙伴协作，推进其余报告和补丁的提交。
6 月，作为
Patch the Planet 计划
的一部分，我们曾分享 GPT‑5.5 Cyber 已发现 Linux 内核漏洞，并开发了 24 个本地权限提升利用程序，用于验证和报告这些漏洞。我们将这项工作扩展为一条由即将推出的网络安全模型驱动的流水线，涵盖漏洞发现、动态验证、可利用性评估和补丁生成。流水线运行结束后，研究人员审核了输出结果，并将发现的漏洞连同补丁一并提交。
摘要
研究方法
我们的流水线大致按以下流程运行：首先识别 Linux 内核中与安全相关的部分，对这些审计目标进行静态扫描，找出疑似漏洞；随后在隔离环境中动态复现，创建概念验证（PoC）利用程序以证明其可利用性，再生成补丁；最后由安全研究人员审核结果。
流水线的输出包括根因分析、可触发崩溃的最小概念验证程序、候选补丁和完整的漏洞利用程序，帮助研究人员评估漏洞的严重程度，并将修复提交至上游。
研究发现
在 2026 年 10 月中旬的一次运行中，我们的流水线使用一款即将推出的网络安全模型，动态复现了 1,724 个漏洞，并针对一个常用 Linux 发行版，为
291 个信息泄露
漏洞生成了 PoC，同时生成了
948 个有效的本地权限提升
（LPE）利用程序。此次运行共消耗价值 1,213,430 美元的 API 额度，即
每个 LPE 利用程序的成本为 1,279 美元。
目标虚拟机运行的是标准桌面操作系统，而非刻意弱化防护的目标，采用的威胁模型与网络安全竞赛（如
Pwn2Own
⁠
（在新窗口中打开）
、
TyphoonPWN
⁠
（在新窗口中打开）
）相同。Pwn2Own 和 TyphoonPWN 过去曾分别为 Linux 内核 LPE 利用程序提供 20,000 美元和 70,000 美元的漏洞赏金。按这些历史赏金金额估算，948 个利用程序的假设价值为
1,890 万至 6,630 万美元
，约为流水线运行成本的
16 至 55 倍
。
在经过适配的
kernelCTF
⁠
（在新窗口中打开）
环境中，该环境使用缩小了攻击面的 Linux 内核版本，我们的流水线获得了
25 个信息泄露 PoC
和
21 个 LPE 利用程序
。作为对比，截至撰写本文时，kernelCTF 在 2026 年已接收 26 个经确认的零日 LPE 利用程序。
此次测试消耗了价值约 32,936 美元的 API 额度。如果这 21 个漏洞均被该计划接收，将获得约
150 万美元赏金
，为扫描成本的
约 45 倍
。
据我们所知，流水线中的智能体发现并使用了至少 10 种全新的 Linux 漏洞利用技术。
研究思考
Linux 维护者和安全社区正在努力加快漏洞的发现与修复。在扫描运行的 10 天内，我们观察到超过 100 个 Linux LPE 漏洞已获修复，或已有其他贡献者提交了待合入的补丁，另有约 300 个正在公开讨论中。
考虑到前沿模型发现漏洞的速度，我们认为，自动生成补丁对于以所需速度保障软件安全、缩短漏洞可被利用的时间窗口至关重要。我们相信，在人类专家指导下迭代，AI 生成的补丁能够做到功能正确、符合现有代码风格，并能抵御攻击变体。这是值得进一步研究的重要方向。
更强大的模型能够在现有代码中发现新漏洞，其中往往包括潜藏更久、更难识别的漏洞。尽管两次扫描之间经过了三个月的安全加固，我们在 10 月中旬使用较新网络安全模型的分析流水线所发现的新 LPE 漏洞数量，仍超过 7 月 GPT‑5.6 Sol 运行结果的 5 倍。
大型复杂软件项目可能需要多轮扫描和漏洞修复，才能将潜藏的缺陷“挖到底”。理想情况下，每推出新一代前沿模型，都应重复这一过程。这一点既适用于专有软件，也适用于开源软件。
在短期和中期内，如果操作系统未及时安装最新可用补丁，那么对于资源充足的威胁行为者而言，获得其中一个低权限账户，实际上就应被视为等同于获得 root 权限。纵深防御，以及使用沙箱和 Firecracker、gVisor 等隔离方案，对于限制漏洞被利用后的影响范围十分重要。
我们认为，在未来几年内，只要某个软件项目存在漏洞，前沿模型就很可能能够发现它们；而在漏洞披露后，即使能力较弱的模型也可能开发出利用程序。在一个没有未知漏洞的世界里，构建和维护高保障软件将至关重要，尤其是操作系统、浏览器、图像解析库、TCP/IP 协议栈等核心软件。除了发现和修复现有漏洞，投入资源训练模型，使其默认编写安全代码，通过移除不必要的功能来缩小攻击面，以及开展形式化验证，都是有望有效扩大软件安全保障规模的未来研究方向。
为何选择 Linux 内核
Linux 内核支撑着 Android 设备、云基础设施、超级计算机，以及数十亿人使用的其他系统。内核拥有超过 4,000 万行代码，通过系统调用、网络、文件系统和设备驱动程序暴露出广泛的攻击面。我们选择 Linux，是为了研究前沿模型在如此庞大且重要的代码库中，发现漏洞并证明其安全影响的效果。
最初的漏洞发现阶段产出了数千个疑似漏洞，数量之多使安全研究人员无法逐一手动审核和分诊。漏洞发现流水线在实际运行中的挑战，不在于发现漏洞，而在于确定哪些问题能够复现、它们突破了什么安全边界，以及哪些最值得维护者优先关注。
成本分析
OpenAI 网络安全团队的使命，是帮助保障全球赖以运行的软件的安全。我们公布各阶段的 API 成本，以帮助研究人员评估复现和扩展这项工作所需的资源。这些成本对应的是本次评估所使用的模型、目标配置和工作流。我们更广泛的目标，是帮助防御者发现并修复漏洞，减少攻击者可乘之机，提高其利用软件漏洞的成本。
最后需要说明的是，本次研究侧重于方法和模型能力测量，而非成本。我们预计，对执行框架进行充分的工程优化，能够显著降低各阶段的成本；因此，我们报告的成本更接近一个上限。
漏洞研究流水线
我们的漏洞研究原型是一条包含五个阶段的流水线，以一款即将推出的网络安全模型为核心：
漏洞发现：
智能体识别代码库中与安全相关的部分，并扫描其中的疑似漏洞。
动态验证：
智能体尝试在隔离环境中复现每个疑似漏洞，并保留运行时证据。这一步输出已复现并验证的漏洞。
可利用性评估：
智能体测试已验证的漏洞是否能够造成信息泄露或本地权限提升。
补丁生成
：智能体为每个已识别的漏洞生成修复补丁。
人工审核
：安全研究人员在向维护者报告之前，审核利用程序、补丁和建议的严重程度评级。
流水线结束时，系统会汇总根因分析、可触发崩溃的最小概念验证程序、候选补丁和完整的漏洞利用程序，帮助研究人员评估漏洞的严重程度，并将修复提交至上游。
漏洞发现
Linux 内核中的代码并非每一行都与安全相关。我们的流水线使用一组侦察智能体识别高价值审计目标，再将其交给分析智能体进行漏洞扫描。
侦察智能体
侦察智能体逐一阅读文件夹和文件，根据可达性（低权限用户是否可达）及安全相关性，确定需要审计的目标。
这一阶段识别出 5,034 个审计目标，约 280 万行代码，占整个 Linux 内核代码库的约 7%。与分析完整代码库相比，这显著降低了安全审计的成本。这一步消耗了价值 3,426 美元的 API 额度。

分析智能体
接下来，分析智能体使用类似于
Codex Security 插件
⁠
（在新窗口中打开）
的工作流，分析每个审计目标并找出疑似漏洞。总体而言，分析智能体会阅读分配给它的审计目标代码，理解其工作原理、确定其威胁模型，并查找其中的漏洞。
在 12 小时内，分析智能体找出了去重后共计 2,308 个疑似漏洞。这一阶段消耗了价值 316,549 美元的 API 额度。
漏洞验证
疑似漏洞不等于已验证的漏洞。面对如此规模，我们的研究团队无法逐一手动调查每份报告。
因此，我们重点验证满足以下条件的疑似漏洞：a）低权限用户可达；b）不需要特殊权能；c）能产生可测量的内存损坏证据。
对于每个疑似漏洞，分诊智能体都会生成概念验证程序，并在隔离虚拟机中运行。该虚拟机的 Linux 内核启用了内核地址检测器（KASAN）。智能体同时观察程序输出和系统控制台，不断改进概念验证程序，直到复现报告中的行为，或穷尽可能的触发方式。
在 30 小时内，我们的系统复现了 1,724 个漏洞，约占 2,308 个疑似漏洞的 74.7%。单靠静态代码审查容易产生误报。因此，分析智能体的准确性，以及分诊智能体自主为近四分之三的疑似漏洞创建有效概念验证程序的能力，都令我们印象深刻。
其余疑似漏洞中，大多数要么需要更高权限，要么因为难以触发的竞态条件、特定触发条件（例如要求某一行发生内存分配失败），或验证耗时过长（例如引用计数回绕），而未能在限定时间内复现。仅有 3.1% 属于模型分析错误，即报告的漏洞依赖于不可能成立的条件。
验证阶段共消耗了价值 73,330 美元的 API 额度。我们观察到，验证流水线需要生成概念验证程序来确认疑似漏洞是否真实存在，这一过程比仅基于静态分析提出建议的成本更高，而且尝试验证真实漏洞与误报的成本相近。因此，在流水线的较早阶段排除误报，能显著提高整个流程的成本效益。
可利用性评估
验证能够确认漏洞真实存在，却不能确定修复它有多紧迫。例如，与只能导致本地拒绝服务的漏洞相比，能够实现本地权限提升的漏洞应享有更高优先级。验证了 1,724 个漏洞后，下一项任务是找出潜在安全影响最大的漏洞。
初筛智能体对每份报告、崩溃日志及相关源代码进行静态审查。我们刻意采用宽松的筛选标准，避免遗漏可能严重的问题，同时排除没有合理利用路径的情况。由此，结果缩小至 313 个信息泄露候选项和 1,238 个本地权限提升候选项。
随后，漏洞利用开发（ExploitDev）智能体在隔离虚拟机中测试这些候选项。虚拟机启用了标准 Linux 发行版的防护措施，包括管理模式执行保护（SMEP）、管理模式访问保护（SMAP）、内核地址空间布局随机化（KASLR）和 HARDENED_USERCOPY。这有助于避免因禁用防护措施而得出不切实际的评估结果。
智能体生成了 291 个信息泄露概念验证程序，以及 1,169 个有效的本地权限提升利用程序，后者可使无特权的本地用户获得 root 权限。
我们进行了变体分析，并针对这些利用程序背后的漏洞开发了 948 个不同的补丁。我们以此数量确定去重后的 LPE 漏洞总数。成功利用程序的平均开发成本为价值 359 美元的额度。这使防御者能够以相对较低的成本，测试已发现漏洞的可利用性。
漏洞初筛智能体消耗了价值 44,194 美元的 API 额度。漏洞利用阶段共消耗了价值 775,929 美元的 API 额度，其中处理信息泄露候选项耗费 84,929 美元，处理本地权限提升候选项耗费 691,000 美元。
平均而言，处理一个本地权限提升候选项的成本为 558 美元，约为处理一个信息泄露候选项（271 美元）的两倍。这是因为信息泄露 PoC 沿用了验证阶段的成果，只需较少修改即可用于漏洞利用。相比之下，从 LPE 候选项开发利用程序需要许多额外步骤，例如规划利用策略、确定可利用的脆弱对象、绕过缓解措施等。我们还注意到，未成功的利用尝试（69 个案例，平均 3,922 美元）的成本远高于成功的尝试（1,169 个案例，平均 360 美元）。这主要是由少数难以利用的漏洞（例如竞态条件）造成的。如果定义合理的放弃条件，例如一小时内没有进展就停止尝试，就能显著降低 ExploitDev 的成本。
补丁生成
系统还会为每个已验证的漏洞生成补丁。我们向模型提供相关源代码，并通过提示说明补丁编写的最佳实践，例如对补丁执行静态检查、遵循周边代码采用的软件开发规范，以及进行变体分析以确保修补完整。
按照 Linux 内核社区的建议，我们已针对关键漏洞提交了数百份报告和补丁，并正与
Patch the Planet
合作伙伴协作，逐步提交其余补丁。这项工作是我们通过
Daybreak
支持开源项目的更广泛承诺的一部分。
研究发现
本节分享这项研究的经验、思考及进一步分析。
维护者正在迅速修补漏洞
在研究过程中，我们观察到 Linux 维护者正迅速采取行动，修复漏洞、保护用户。扫描于 2026 年 10 月中旬针对当时最新的 Linux 内核开展。10 天后，自主扫描和人工分析完成时，已有 61 个 LPE 漏洞在上游得到修复，43 个已有待合入的补丁，299 个正在被公开报告和讨论。
我们衷心感谢加紧修补已发现问题的 Linux 维护者，以及积极贡献研究发现的广大安全社区成员。保障全球软件安全，正需要这样的共同努力。漏洞披露和修补的快速推进，也凸显了用户和企业及时更新软件的重要性。
启示
：自动化分诊应考虑快速的补丁更新周期。基于最新代码重新验证发现的问题，包括初次扫描后新合入的代码，有助于避免重复或过时的报告。这样能将注意力集中在尚未解决的漏洞上，为维护者提供可据以采取行动的证据，同时避免增加不必要的审核负担。
更强大的模型发现更多漏洞
在开发流水线期间，2026 年 7 月下旬，GPT‑5.6 Sol 发现并利用了 166 个不同的 LPE 漏洞，全流程消耗了价值 513,690 美元的 API 额度。
在 2026 年 10 月中旬的第二次扫描中，较新的网络安全模型发现并利用了 948 个不同的 LPE 漏洞，全流程消耗了价值 1,213,430 美元的 API 额度。两次测试扫描的都是当时最新的 Linux 内核 master 分支。
启示
：随着模型能力提升，应重新扫描此前审计过的代码。即使使用相同的研究执行框架，更强大的模型也可能发现早期模型遗漏的漏洞。
全新的漏洞利用技术
我们抽取了智能体开发的 166 个利用程序，分析其中采用的漏洞利用技术。据我们所知，智能体在这些样本中使用了 10 种全新的漏洞利用技术。我们与第三方内核漏洞利用专家分享了这些技术，对他们而言，这些技术也都是全新的。
这 10 种技术中，两种涉及新的持久弹性对象，模型用它们在目标内核缓存中进行对象喷射；两种是新的内存页布局操控技术，用于提高利用的可靠性；五种是新的纯数据攻击技术，可直接或通过任意写实现权限提升；另一种涉及任意类型混淆。出于安全考虑，本文不公开这些新漏洞利用技术的完整技术细节。
启示
：前沿模型并非只会匹配已知的易受攻击代码模式，或仅使用已知的漏洞利用技术；它们展现出了创造力，能够提出新方法。
漏洞利用成本能给防御者带来哪些启示
衡量发现和利用漏洞的成本，并据此指导防御投入，是我们团队使命的重要组成部分。我们的目标是帮助防御者在攻击者利用漏洞之前修复它们，并让攻击者利用软件漏洞的成本高到难以承受。衡量漏洞利用成本，有助于评估这一挑战如何随模型能力提升而变化。本节将流水线的运行成本，与漏洞赏金计划为所发现漏洞提供的奖励进行比较。
实验中的目标虚拟机运行的是标准桌面操作系统，而非刻意弱化防护的目标，采用的威胁模型与网络安全竞赛（如
Pwn2Own

、
TyphoonPWN

我们还针对 Google 的
kernelCTF

漏洞奖励计划测试了流水线。该计划以经过加固、攻击面缩小的 Linux 内核为目标。
我们在 kernelCTF 环境中，针对最新版本的 Linux 内核运行了流水线，获得了 25 个信息泄露概念验证程序和 21 个本地权限提升利用程序。由于该内核与 kernelCTF 的 SLAB_VIRTUAL 缓解措施不兼容，我们从配置中移除了这一项。作为对比，截至撰写本文时，kernelCTF 在 2026 年已接收 26 个经确认的零日 LPE 利用程序。整个测试共持续 112 小时，消耗了价值约 32,936 美元的 API 额度，其中漏洞发现占 API 成本的 83.7%。如果这 21 个漏洞均被该计划接收，将获得约 150 万美元赏金，约为成本的 45 倍。
启示：
按照公开的赏金金额计算，使用当前具备网络安全能力的模型，我们的漏洞研究流水线在本次研究时已可实现净盈利。防御者应主动分析自身软件，让攻击者利用漏洞的成本高到难以承受。
用错了零日漏洞
在可利用性评估期间，漏洞利用开发（ExploitDev）智能体会收到一份漏洞报告，并被要求创建功能完整的利用程序。只要成功获得 root shell，流水线就会将该漏洞标记为已利用。在早期的一次运行中，漏洞利用阶段报告了 200 个成功的本地权限提升利用程序。然而，经人工审核，我们发现其中 20 个是
通过另一个零日漏洞
获得 root 权限的，而非通过分配给它们的漏洞。这表明，即使智能体成功完成了漏洞利用，也仍需适当验证。
随后，我们收紧了任务约束，并增加独立检查，确认每个最终利用程序使用的确实是分配给它的漏洞。
启示
：在自主安全研究中，除了验证结果本身，还要验证达成结果的路径；隔离、监控和独立检查都是必要的控制措施。
更强大的模型可能只需更轻量的编排
在研究初期，我们探讨了一项设计决策：是否应围绕智能体构建复杂的编排机制，以增强其网络安全能力。结果表明，更强大的模型所需的编排和逐步引导更少。而额外带来的提升不足以抵消维护成本。因此，我们决定移除复杂的编排机制。
实验对比了 GPT‑5.5 Cyber 和 GPT‑5.6 Cyber。我们观察到，GPT‑5.5 Cyber 无法始终准确判断何时以及如何应用现有的 Linux 内核漏洞利用技术。于是，我们将 103 种技术整理为便于模型使用的格式，放入智能体环境，并通过提示引导智能体使用。在 63 个候选利用目标中，这使成功率从 76.2% 提高到了 88.9%。
使用 GPT‑5.6 Cyber 重复实验时，模型能够更好地自行查找、选择和应用相关技术。我们移除了技术和技能编排机制，而采用轻量编排的 GPT‑5.6 Cyber 工作流，表现优于辅助机制更复杂的 GPT‑5.5 Cyber 工作流。为 GPT‑5.6 Cyber 重新加入额外的技术层，仅带来了 1.5 个百分点的微小提升。
启示
：随着基础模型能力变化，应重新评估编排机制和执行框架。对某一代模型帮助显著的辅助机制，对更强的模型可能价值有限，应权衡其收益与维护成本。
通过迭代改进补丁生成
最初，当我们直接提示模型生成候选补丁时，它能够生成在功能上正确、可阻止概念验证程序触发问题的补丁，但偶尔也会引入其他问题：代码冗余、可能牺牲性能、偏离编码规范，或未检查相关代码中同一漏洞的变体，导致修补不完整。
增加指令并迭代补丁生成流程后，补丁质量得到了提升。这表明，通过适当引导，AI 生成的安全补丁有可能做到正确、精简，并符合现有编码规范。这一领域的研究仍在积极推进，我们相信，随着未来模型的发展，这项工作会变得更容易、更有效。在少数情况下，我们的研究原型还发现了人类专家编写的补丁中的问题，使这些问题得以在补丁合入前修复。
启示
：模型可以加快修补流程，但补丁编写技能和执行框架可能需要迭代，才能确保补丁可靠地满足功能与非功能要求。此外，我们建议使用模型对人工及 AI 生成的补丁进行对抗性审查，以发现补丁可被绕过、遗漏其他攻击路径或变体等问题。
测试基础设施中的漏洞
在 kernelCTF 测试中，除了 21 个 Linux 内核零日漏洞利用程序，我们的研究原型还发现并利用了一个 QEMU TCG 漏洞。分析智能体被分配去分析系统调用入口代码，在编写程序测试权限切换时，遇到了意料之外的内核崩溃。它对崩溃进行了排查，在无法访问 QEMU 源代码的情况下，将问题追溯至 QEMU TCG，并将该漏洞写入报告。随后，ExploitDev 智能体成功为该漏洞开发了本地权限提升利用程序。我们在手动分析利用程序时发现了这个 QEMU 漏洞，并确认它已在上游 QEMU 中修复，但实验所用的发布构建版本尚未包含该修复。
启示
：具备网络安全能力的前沿模型能够发现测试基础设施中的漏洞。我们建议在开展进攻性漏洞研究之前，测试基础设施的每个组成部分。我们已
主动测试自身基础设施
，披露并修补了 Kata、Moby/Docker、gVisor 及其他项目中的许多漏洞。
结语
我们的目标是将模型日益增强的能力，转化为互联网安全守护者的长期优势。这项研究表明，前沿模型不断提升的网络安全能力，可以有效用于查找 Linux 内核等复杂软件中的漏洞。加固 Linux 及其他开源项目等关键软件项目，能够保护众多下游系统和用户。
我们希望通过
Daybreak 计划
旗下的
Patch the Planet
，将这项研究扩展到更多关键软件项目，并与维护者和安全合作伙伴共同开发可靠的自动化修补方案。我们希望持续减少攻击者可乘之机，提高发现和利用漏洞的成本，直至预期收益不再值得发动攻击。
每一代模型都应帮助我们构建让下一代模型更难攻破的软件。我们将继续努力，构建一个安全的互联网，让每个人都能在其上尽情创造。

items.content:
01
Summary
Johannes Hermle*, Ben Jones*, Lukas Althoff*, Ryan Heller, Thomas Lyttelton, Carolyn Stein, Nathan Wilmers, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory
*Lead authors of the report
Summary
What we measure.
AI could speed up scientific discovery, but by how much depends on what AI can do and how scientists use it. Using privacy-preserving methods, we study 207,000 Claude and Claude Code research sessions to understand how Claude is used across scientific fields and research tasks. We are conducting this research to help the public better understand the state of AI for science today and assess the impact that AI may have on scientific discovery in the future.
Where scientists use Claude.
Relative to the number of researchers in each field, Claude is used more in the formal sciences, such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics, and less in health and lab-based physical sciences. Scientists primarily use Claude to analyze data and to write. Data analysis alone accounts for about one-third of sessions on Claude and nearly half of sessions on Claude Code. Scientists use it less for idea generation and data gathering, even though, in an accompanying survey, they rank those tasks as the most important for scientific discovery. That said, specialized AI tools designed for scientific work could narrow the gap between the research tasks scientists use AI for and the ones they consider most important. On Claude Science, for instance, idea generation makes up about twice the share of use that it does on Claude.
How Claude use tracks AI capability.
We create a measure of how well AI can, in theory, perform each research task. The tasks AI is best suited to (the top 20% on this measure) get two to four times as much Claude use as the time researchers spend on them would predict. The tasks AI is least suited to (the bottom 20%), which include most physical work, get very little. We observe the same pattern across fields: fields where AI can perform many tasks well, such as computer science and statistics, use Claude more.
What this could mean for the speed of scientific discovery.
Using a simple model, we explore scenarios for how much AI could speed up research. If existing AI capabilities are widely adopted, they could double research output in some fields. If AI could carry out all non-physical research work, output in fields such as computer science and statistics could rise as much as 15-fold, while output in bench sciences such as chemistry and biology, which are held back by physical bottlenecks, would rise three- or fourfold. In our survey of researchers who actively use AI, about 40% expect AI models to carry out full research projects on their own by 2030.
Introduction
Science has been described as an “endless frontier” (Bush 1945). But how fast we explore that frontier has historically been limited by a scarce resource: the time and talent of human researchers. Artificial intelligence could ease that limit by amplifying what researchers can do, transforming both the process of discovery and the pace of exploration (Wang et al. 2023; Amodei 2024). Few applications of AI could matter more for human welfare. Given the highly cognitive nature of research compared with most sectors of the economy, AI’s effects may be particularly large and early in this domain.
Recent examples show AI playing a growing role in scientific discovery. In structural biology, AlphaFold predicted the three-dimensional shapes of over 200 million proteins (Jumper et al. 2021; Varadi et al. 2024), and its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In materials science, GNoME predicted 380,000 stable new crystals (Merchant et al. 2023). In mathematics, researchers have used AI systems to help resolve decades-old Erdős problems, produce a potential proof for a Millennium Prize problem, and make progress on other major problems, from open conjectures to verifying landmark proofs (Anthropic 2026a, 2026b; OpenAI 2026a, 2026b; Tsoukalas et al. 2026).
Beyond these developments, most scientific progress involves many specialized, interlinked research tasks, which can vary substantially across fields. How much AI accelerates scientific discovery depends not only on AI’s capabilities, but also on how it is adopted across these tasks. In this report, we use privacy-preserving infrastructure to study the scientific use of Claude, Claude Code, and Claude Science. We document how usage varies across fields and tasks, identify what explains these usage patterns, and outline scenarios for how AI could accelerate research.
Claude use in science varies by field. Relative to their number of researchers, formal sciences such as computer science, mathematics, and statistics use Claude more heavily, while health and lab-based physical sciences use it less. Across research tasks, scientists use Claude more for analyzing data and writing, and less for gathering data or generating ideas and hypotheses. This is consistent with self-reported AI use from an accompanying survey of scientists.
To understand these differences, we develop a measure of theoretical AI capability. Claude use is higher in tasks and fields that score higher on this measure. These also tend to be more cognitive in nature and better suited to reinforcement learning, in which AI learns from feedback on repeated attempts. In short, scientists appear to use AI where it works best.
Based on these findings, we outline scenarios for how AI could accelerate scientific progress. With current capabilities, research output in some fields could as much as double, primarily from task-level augmentation. Researchers in our survey expect much greater capabilities to come. In a hypothetical scenario where AI fully automates all non-physical work, highly cognitive fields such as computer science or statistics could see up to a 15-fold increase in output. Because the fields with the largest potential for acceleration include those that produce AI itself, these gains could create an additional feedback loop, in which faster AI research produces more capable AI, which in turn could further accelerate research.
While faster scientific discovery could bring substantial benefits to humanity, AI-driven research also carries risks and uncertainties. Less human oversight could lead to the pursuit of dangerous or unethical research. AI could also reshape researchers’ careers, making research work more or less rewarding, and alter the sense of purpose associated with the human pursuit of knowledge.
How we conducted this research
Our goal with this research is to measure the different ways scientists use Claude while protecting the details of their work. To do this, we use privacy-preserving infrastructure to analyze the scientific use of Claude on consumer plans. A language model, used here as a “classifier,” reads each session transcript and labels it with a fixed set of categories, such as the field and the research task it involves, according to a predefined taxonomy (SciNet taxonomy by Alamos and Althoff 2026). The resulting labels, such as “chemistry” or “data cleaning,” are the only information from these conversations retained and analyzed by the research team for this report. No classifier employed in this study extracts and stores open-ended information or details on research content, such as research datasets, hypotheses, experimental methods, early findings, or unpublished papers. Results are reported only in aggregate and only for cells that meet a minimum number of distinct accounts. All classifiers introduced in this study are listed in the
Appendix
.
Our measurement involves two steps. A first classifier identifies whether a session transcript involves scientific work. A second classifier then assigns each of these transcripts to a field, subfield, and task in the SciNet taxonomy. SciNet contains 7,262 tasks, spanning 34 fields and 318 subfields. Some tasks in the taxonomy, such as drafting manuscripts, are universal to all fields. Others are specific to individual fields or subfields. For instance, in the taxonomy, the task of predicting optical absorption and emission spectra is specific to materials science. Together, the tasks cover the full process of producing a new research finding.
Our main sample consists of 207,049 sessions on consumer plans from August 2 to September 30, 2026, which were assigned a scientific field and a research task: 128,914 from Chat and Cowork, two general-purpose interfaces for conversation and knowledge work, hereafter referred to as “Claude,” and 78,135 from Claude Code, an agentic coding tool that works directly with a user’s files, writing and running code. We also study a supplemental sample of Claude Science sessions. For details on sample construction, see the
Appendix
.
Combining usage data and a structured taxonomy of research tasks allows us to study which fields adopt Claude and for which parts of the research process. This research contributes to a growing body of work attempting to measure the adoption of AI technology for scientific discovery (Kobak et al. 2025; Liang et al. 2025; Hao et al. 2026; Codreanu et al. 2026).
How Claude use varies across scientific fields
We begin by describing how Claude use varies across scientific fields. Figure 1 compares a field’s share of sessions against the share of global researchers in that field, giving us a sense of relative use per scientific field.
1
On Claude, the three largest fields by session share are computer science (11.9%), engineering (8.4%), and medicine (7.7%), which are also among the largest fields by global researcher counts.
2
Overall, fields with a larger share of researchers also tend to account for a larger share of Claude sessions (log-log correlation of 0.79).
However, Claude use per field cannot be explained by the number of researchers alone. In Figure 1, fields above the 45-degree line show higher usage relative to their size, while fields below the line show lower usage. Relative usage is especially high for the formal sciences, including computer science, mathematics, and statistics. Usage is also high for the social sciences. By contrast, physical sciences such as chemistry, where work often happens in a lab, tend to show lower relative usage. So does medicine, the third-largest field by session volume, where researchers spend much of their time with patients.
On Claude Code, usage is less strongly related to field size (log-log correlation with researcher counts of 0.62) and concentrates in more quantitative fields. Despite making up only 4.3% of the world’s researchers, computer science alone accounts for 32.7% of Claude Code sessions.
3
Other formal sciences, such as mathematics and statistics, also show high relative usage. Relative usage is low in the arts and humanities and in the social sciences, with the exception of economics, a comparatively quantitative field.
Claude use across scientific fields.
Each dot represents a field. The horizontal axis shows the field’s share of researchers, and the vertical axis shows the field’s share of research sessions, both on log scales. The top panel shows sessions from Claude; the bottom panel shows sessions from Claude Code.
We observe similar patterns when comparing usage across 318 subfields within those 34 fields (Figure 2).
4
This more granular subfield view reveals that artificial intelligence and machine learning stands out, with session shares of 5.0% for Claude and 15.2% for Claude Code, despite making up only 1.2% of the world’s researchers. More generally, regardless of the broad scientific domain, computational subfields are among the strongest adopters. These subfields include computational biology, computational linguistics, and computational neuroscience. Robotics also shows high relative usage, likely because it builds heavily on computational methods despite its focus on physical systems.
Claude use across scientific subfields.
Each dot represents a subfield. The horizontal axis shows the subfield’s share of researchers, and the vertical axis shows the subfield’s share of research sessions, both on log scales. The top panel shows sessions from Claude; the bottom panel shows sessions from Claude Code. Subfields with too few accounts are not shown for privacy reasons.
How Claude use varies across research tasks
Beyond understanding which fields use Claude, we also want to understand what scientists use it for. Research involves many different tasks, from generating hypotheses and analyzing data to writing up findings in a research paper. To better discern how Claude supports scientific discovery, we study how usage varies across these tasks. To do so, we assign each session to one of the 7,262 tasks in SciNet. These tasks can be universal to all fields, such as drafting manuscripts, or specific to fields or subfields, such as performing differential gene expression analysis to compare tumor subtypes, which is associated with cancer biology. The taxonomy distinguishes between research tasks, which researchers perform to produce new scientific findings, and non-research tasks, such as teaching, peer review, and service to the department or field.
5
We limit our analysis to research tasks spanning eight categories: (1) data analysis, (2) writing and communication, (3) data gathering, (4) reading and knowledge acquisition, (5) theoretical analysis, (6) design and development (of software, materials, and creative works), (7) ideation and hypothesis generation, and (8) other, such as administering research.
For each task category, we calculate its share of Claude and Claude Code sessions separately. To assess whether usage in a category is high or low, we consider the share of their time that researchers typically spend on that category, as estimated by SciNet. These time estimates are based on an LLM classifier, validated using both wet-lab research protocols that record researcher time spent per task and the frequency of tasks across thousands of academic papers (see the
Appendix
). This provides a benchmark to assess whether the share of Claude use across different task categories follows or deviates from how researchers spend their time.
Usage by task category.
Data analysis tasks have the highest usage in absolute terms and are overrepresented relative to researcher time. Data analysis accounts for 33.7% of sessions on Claude and 48.1% on Claude Code, compared with 27.6% of researcher time. Writing and communication tasks also show high usage, especially on Claude (32.0%, compared with 16.0% of researcher time).
6
Data gathering tasks have low relative usage, accounting for 28.6% of researcher time but only 11.5% of sessions on Claude and 11.9% on Claude Code. The underrepresentation of data gathering is particularly strong for tasks with physical barriers, such as the collection of clinical or biochemical data. Data gathering tasks that can rely on more digital processes, such as retrieving archival documents or text, are less underrepresented, while purely digital data collection tasks, such as collecting online data, can be overrepresented. Ideation and hypothesis generation tasks also have low usage, accounting for 4.2% of sessions on Claude and 2.1% on Claude Code, compared with 7.1% of researcher time.
Claude use by scientific task category.
Each row represents one of the eight task categories. Orange bars represent the share of Claude research sessions dedicated to each category; blue bars represent the same for Claude Code research sessions. The black lines represent the estimated share of research time calculated from SciNet (see the
Appendix
).
Comparing observed usage to survey evidence.
Along with our analysis of Claude and Claude Code sessions, we conducted a survey of 528 scientists, whose self-reported AI usage lines up with the patterns we observed in those sessions. The sample consists of researchers primarily in the life and health sciences who are active adopters of AI.
7
Consistent with the Claude usage patterns shown in Figure 3, survey participants’ self-reported AI usage is highest for data analysis and writing and communication, and lower for ideation and hypothesis generation and data gathering. Participants also report more shared or delegated use of AI for data analysis and writing and communication (Figure 4).
The survey also asked which categories matter most for producing important research results. Respondents rank ideation and hypothesis generation first and data gathering second. Notably, these categories are underrepresented in self-reported usage as well as in Claude sessions. The reasons for this underrepresentation likely differ. Much of data gathering is physical, while ideation is not. For ideation, scientists may prefer generating ideas themselves, or they may perceive AI’s capabilities as limited. Our data may also undercount ideation, since it tends to be woven into many other research tasks and is difficult to classify. But AI may also be genuinely weaker at high-level ideation, such as choosing which research question to pursue and designing a study to answer it.
Researchers’ reported use of AI.
The left panel shows the percentage of survey respondents at each level of AI use, from none to autonomous, for four research task categories. The right panel shows how the respondents rate the importance of each category for producing an important research result (allocating 100 points across the four categories).
Biological and biomedical use of Claude Science.
While Claude and Claude Code are general-purpose interfaces, specialized AI tools for the sciences are increasingly available. To study whether such tools support more specialized and demanding research, we use our privacy-preserving analysis infrastructure to compare biology and biomedical work on Claude Science with that on Claude and Claude Code.
Claude Science connects Claude to many research tools and databases that are otherwise fragmented and acts to integrate and accelerate scientific workflows. Scientists must often use different platforms, each with unique data structures or query languages, to combine distinct tools and databases in their research. For example, biologists studying whether existing drugs can act on a specific protein must typically consult separate databases regarding the protein’s function, its structure, compounds already tested against it, and related drug trials or papers. Claude Science combines these into one workflow.
Use of Claude Science is concentrated in the life sciences. The top two fields are biomedical sciences and biology, which together comprise over 50% of sessions. Within these fields, we assess which tasks are most overrepresented relative to tasks performed by Claude.
We find that researchers use Claude Science for more specialized tasks than Claude (Figure 5). For example, the task “Propose mechanistic models for protein–protein or protein–ligand interactions” is 5.6x more likely to appear on Claude Science than on Claude. This task involves explaining, at the level of individual molecular contacts, how a protein binds to another protein or to a small molecule such as a drug. Claude Science is well positioned for this task, as it can gather protein structures and binding data from multiple connected databases and combine them into a testable model of the interaction. By contrast, Claude Science is used relatively less for general tasks such as drafting manuscripts or coordinating with collaborators. Moreover, we find that ideation and hypothesis generation accounts for 8% of Claude Science sessions, roughly on par with the share of researcher time these tasks take, suggesting that specialized AI tools for science can facilitate more complex and creative work.
Claude Science use across fields and tasks.
The top panel shows the top 10 fields by their share of all Claude Science research sessions. The bottom panel shows the most and least typical tasks on Claude Science relative to Claude within biology and biomedical sciences specifically, calculated as follows: (task’s share of Claude Science research sessions in these fields) / (its share of Claude research sessions in these fields).
Focusing on biomedical sciences and biology, and using measures from our economic primitives framework introduced in
prior work
(Appel et al. 2026), we find that tasks on Claude Science are longer, more sophisticated, and performed more autonomously than those on Claude and Claude Code (Figure 6). This is consistent with specialized AI tools being used for more demanding tasks.
8
Sessions on Claude Science contain work that would take nearly twice as many human hours to complete without AI as work on Claude and Claude Code. The content of these sessions is also more advanced. Over 80% of Claude Science use is estimated to require doctoral-level training (20 years of education), compared with about 50–70% on other interfaces. Over 70% of Claude Science sessions are performed with a high degree of AI autonomy, far higher than on Claude (23.7%) and somewhat higher than on Claude Code (64.1%).
Use characteristics in biology and biomedical sciences.
Comparing human task time, doctoral-level content, and level of autonomy for tasks completed on Claude, Claude Code, and Claude Science in biology and biomedical sciences. The hatched orange and blue bars reweight the subfields and tasks performed by Claude and Claude Code to match those performed by Claude Science.
Outputs of Claude use.
Finally, the artifacts produced with Claude show clear differences across fields (Figure 7).
9
Written artifacts such as documents, reports, or academic papers are more common in the social sciences and humanities, relative to the natural and formal sciences. Conversely, technical artifacts such as code, software outputs, and data are more frequent in the natural and formal sciences. The health sciences overall are more similar to the social sciences in terms of artifacts produced. Technical artifacts are about twice as common on Claude Code as on Claude, but the broad pattern across fields is similar (see the
Appendix
).
Artifacts produced by Claude.
The share of sessions on Claude that produce written artifacts and technical artifacts by field. Fields are ordered by the difference between the share of written artifacts and technical artifacts.
How use relates to capabilities
Does AI usage track AI capabilities? Field size explains some of the variation in Claude use, but not all of it. For example, researchers in computer science use Claude far more than the field’s size predicts, while those in nutrition use Claude far less. Similarly, where researchers spend their own time does not fully predict where they use Claude the most. Some broad task categories, such as data analysis and writing, have a much larger share of usage than of research time, while others, such as data gathering and ideation and hypothesis generation, have a much smaller share. Here, we test whether these differences in usage reflect what AI can actually do.
To measure task-specific AI capabilities, we first construct capability scores using an LLM classifier. For each task, SciNet provides a list of individual steps that a scientist needs to perform to complete the task. For instance, in chemistry, one task involves purifying reaction mixtures, and one of that task’s steps involves packing a chromatography column. The classifier is shown pairs of steps across the taxonomy and asked which one AI can perform better. We aggregate these comparisons using a Bradley–Terry model—the same model behind the Elo ratings that rank chess players based on head-to-head results. A step’s score rises when it wins comparisons and falls when it loses them. We then average each task’s steps to obtain a task-level score (see the
Appendix
for details). We label this measure
theoretical AI capability
. We refer to a task’s specific score as its
AI capability score
.
To compare usage across tasks, we ask whether Claude use is higher or lower for a task, relative to the time researchers spend on that task. For example, a task that takes 5% of researchers’ time but accounts for 10% of Claude sessions would represent twice as much use as expected, a ratio of 2. A ratio of 1 indicates that Claude use is in line with researcher time spent on the task. A ratio below 1 indicates that Claude is used less than expected based on the amount of researcher time the task takes.
Figure 8 shows that this use ratio rises sharply with a task’s AI capability score. For tasks in the lowest 20% of capability scores, like purifying reaction mixtures and conducting participant observation, Claude is barely used. At median capability scores, the ratio is roughly 1, so usage is in line with researcher time. For tasks in the top 20% of capability scores, like visualizing data and applying statistical tests, usage is about twice as high on Claude and about four times as high on Claude Code, compared with the typical time researchers spend on those tasks. These patterns suggest that scientists’ use of Claude closely tracks AI capability scores. The steeper gradient for Claude Code reflects its focus on computational work, which has higher capability scores.
Claude use and theoretical AI capability.
The vertical axis represents the use ratio for the tasks in each capability quintile, calculated as the share of research sessions devoted to those tasks divided by their share of research time estimated from SciNet. The horizontal axis represents the task’s AI capability score (percentile). The orange dots represent the average use ratio for tasks in each AI capability quintile for Claude; the blue dots represent the same for Claude Code.
Theoretical AI capabilities can differ across tasks for many reasons. To understand these differences, we relate each task’s AI capability score to three groups of LLM-derived task characteristics: its suitability for reinforcement learning (RL); whether the work is predominantly cognitive, interpersonal, or physical; and whether regulatory restrictions limit AI use (Figure 9; see the
Appendix
for definitions and data sources).
Consider RL suitability. In RL, an AI model tries a task repeatedly and is rewarded when it succeeds, allowing the model to learn how to perform that task. Tasks are particularly suitable for RL when success is easy to verify, when many examples can be simulated in a computing environment, and when feedback can be delivered quickly (Lambert et al. 2024; Guo et al. 2025). We use task-specific measures from SciNet for these three RL-related components and summarize them in a single index. A task’s capability score is highly correlated with its RL index score, which was classified separately (correlation of 0.78). This suggests that AI is most capable at the research tasks where RL is easiest to apply.
Other important task characteristics concern the nature of the work. Some research tasks are fundamentally cognitive, while others require physical actions or interpersonal contact. Physical tasks in general are beyond the reach of purely cognitive machines. There can also be regulatory restrictions that limit AI use. AI capability scores are higher for tasks characterized by cognitive work (correlation of 0.69). By contrast, research tasks that involve more physical work have lower AI capability scores (−0.57). Scores also tend to be lower for research activities that include interpersonal work (−0.31) or that involve regulatory restrictions on AI use (−0.38).
Theoretical AI capability and other task characteristics.
Correlations between a research task’s AI capability score percentile and other characteristics of the task.
The same task characteristics also predict how much researchers use Claude for a given task (Figure 10). Claude is barely used for tasks in the bottom fifth of RL suitability. For tasks in the top fifth, Claude use is disproportionately high relative to the time researchers spend on them: twice as high on Claude, and four times as high on Claude Code. This is similar to the association between Claude use and AI capability scores overall, where the top 20% of tasks also draw two to four times the expected use.
Claude use is also disproportionately high in predominantly cognitive tasks. By contrast, Claude use is low for physical and interpersonal tasks. Claude use is also lower for tasks where regulatory barriers limit AI assistance. Overall, across the spectrum of highly specialized research tasks, usage and capability measures are strongly related.
Claude use and task characteristics.
Each panel considers a different task characteristic. The vertical axes represent the use ratio for groups of tasks (“bins”) with different scores on that characteristic. The horizontal axes represent a measure of the characteristic’s intensity. Orange dots represent the average use ratio for tasks in each bin on Claude; blue dots represent the same for Claude Code. Dots at zero represent bins hidden for privacy because too few accounts are responsible for that use.
Different scientific fields rely on different mixes of research activities. Does the correlation between usage and capability scores for narrow research tasks help explain why some fields use Claude more than others? Our data shows it does: a subfield’s Claude use per researcher tends to rise with the average AI capability score across its tasks (correlations of 0.45 for Claude and 0.57 for Claude Code), as shown in Figure 11.
There is also substantial variation across domains, which suggests that Claude use is affected by factors beyond what AI can do. Health sciences researchers use Claude relatively little compared with the AI capability scores of their tasks, possibly because regulation of medical data and research limits the use of AI or makes it harder to integrate. Researchers in the formal sciences, social sciences, and the arts and humanities use Claude more than the AI capability scores would predict. Much of the work in these fields is done through text and code, which likely facilitates the adoption of AI tools. Claude use in the physical sciences and life sciences generally tracks AI capability scores more closely, though individual subfields can deviate.
Claude use and theoretical AI capability across subfields.
Both panels show each subfield as a dot, sized by the number of researchers in the subfield. The vertical axis shows usage per researcher on a log scale. Usage per researcher is computed as the subfield’s share of research sessions divided by the subfield’s share of total researchers. The horizontal axis shows the subfield’s AI capability score, computed by aggregating across all of the subfield’s research tasks weighted by researcher hours. The black line shows the best fit, and each panel reports the correlation weighted by subfield size. The left panel shows the results for research sessions on Claude; the right panel shows the results for research sessions on Claude Code.
Theoretical AI capability also predicts how much researchers allow Claude to work autonomously. Figure 12 shows that autonomous use correlates with the theoretical AI capability of the subfield. In other words, not only do subfields with more theoretical AI capability use AI more, but they also use it in a more autonomous manner.
AI autonomy and theoretical AI capability across subfields.
Both panels show each subfield as a dot, sized by the number of researchers in the subfield. The left panel represents research sessions on Claude; the right panel represents research sessions on Claude Code. The vertical axis shows the mean autonomy score for sessions in the subfield, weighted by session volume. The horizontal axis shows the mean theoretical capability of the subfield’s tasks, also weighted by usage. Tasks that are not covered by any session are excluded from the analysis, since they cannot be scored on autonomy. For legibility, outlier subfields have been dropped, but they are included in the line of best fit and the correlation calculation. Correlations are weighted by subfield size.
Research acceleration scenarios with AI
The pace of scientific and technological progress depends on good ideas and the means to pursue them. Historically, both have been limited by human capacity. There are only so many researchers, and each has only so much time to formulate a hypothesis, design the right tests, run the analyses, and synthesize the findings.
AI could ease these constraints in two ways. First, it could take on work that researchers now do, allowing them to pursue more ideas. Second, it could contribute ideas that researchers might not otherwise identify. The second may ultimately matter most, but it is much harder to measure, so our analysis focuses on the first.
Approach
We consider three scenarios of scientific acceleration through AI. Scenario 1 assumes wide adoption of current AI capabilities, as estimated from our survey and the AI capability scores. Scenarios 2 and 3 are hypothetical futures in which AI fully automates 75% or 100% of non-physical research steps—the individual actions that make up each research task in SciNet—starting with the steps that have the highest AI capability scores. In all three scenarios, researchers continue to perform physical steps. These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts. They show how physical work, theoretical AI capability, and the cost of AI could shape the acceleration of scientific research, and which fields could accelerate the most.
For each scenario, we report two measures. The first is the
AI share
: the fraction of researcher time spent on a study that AI could take on. Given how researchers currently allocate their time, it measures how much human research time AI could free up, and it follows directly from our analyses above. Researchers can redirect that freed-up time to other work, increasing research output. Our second measure, the
acceleration
, estimates this gain: the increase in research output for a fixed research budget, relative to the research output without AI. It tells us how many more research results the same budget could produce. Freed-up time does not translate one-for-one into more output, both because researchers redirect their effort toward the tasks where AI helps less, and because AI itself has costs.
We build the AI share for Scenario 1 from our survey, which records five levels of AI use: none, assistive, shared, delegated, and autonomous. We assume these levels correspond to AI taking on 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of a researcher’s time for a given task step. Within each task category, we rank task steps by AI capability score. We then assign a level of AI use to each task step, in the same proportions reported in our survey, with the highest levels going to the highest-scoring steps. For ideation and hypothesis generation, for example, 17% of responses report no AI use, and 53% report assistive use. The 17% of ideation task steps with the lowest AI capability scores are therefore assigned no AI share, the next 53% are assigned 25%, and so on up the scale. Because respondents are likely to be heavy AI adopters, we treat their reported use as a proxy for what AI can do today. Finally, we aggregate researcher time freed up by AI from steps to fields (see the
Appendix
).
To compute the acceleration, we use an ideas production function, a standard economic model of how research inputs, such as researcher time, are turned into research outputs. In this model, a paper requires many research tasks (Jones 2026). The tasks are complementary, such that strength in one cannot fully make up for weakness in another. As AI makes some tasks cheaper, researchers shift their effort toward tasks where AI helps less, thereby easing the bottlenecks that limit the overall gain. For example, researchers could spend more time coming up with new questions or running more physical experiments to expand empirical evidence. We calibrate how much these bottlenecks limit the overall gain using Ahmadpoor and Jones (2019). For AI’s cost, we assume that an hour of AI agent time costs $30, compared with $95 for an hour of a researcher’s time, and that AI runs for 0.2 hours for each researcher hour it saves. These are illustrative assumptions: the AI cost uses today’s public list prices. The smaller these costs, the more research can be done within a given budget and the larger the acceleration, as we discuss below. The
Appendix
describes the model and assumptions.
Research time freed up by AI and research acceleration.
Every row is a field. The left panel shows fields ranked by the estimated share of researcher time that AI could take on. Circles show estimates for current capabilities; diamonds show the estimated share of time freed up if 75% of non-physical steps are automated; triangles show the estimated share of time freed up if 100% of non-physical steps are automated. The right panel shows the research acceleration given the research budget of a field. Its horizontal axis shows research output with AI as a multiple of the output without AI (1x = no change) under our three scenarios.
Scenario 1: Current capabilities
With current capabilities, if adopted widely, AI could take on 27–52% of the researcher time needed to produce a new study, with a median of 38% across fields (Figure 13, left panel). These shares imply research accelerations ranging from 1.35x in the arts, 1.36x in anthropology, and 1.41x in chemistry to 1.96x in computer science and 2.02x in statistics (Figure 13, right panel). Accelerations remain limited because AI work today is mostly assistive or shared rather than autonomous, so researchers still spend substantial time on nearly every step. Even the most AI-ready fields, whose work is almost entirely cognitive, reach only about a 2x acceleration. These estimates assume that AI diffuses widely and that researchers apply it to every step where it is useful today.
Two factors explain most of the differences across fields. The first is physical work, which AI cannot take on without physical integrations. In lab and field sciences such as the agricultural sciences, biomedical sciences, chemistry, and materials science, 38–41% of researcher time goes to physical steps, compared with 4% in the median field. The physical share alone explains about one-third of the variation in the AI share. The second factor is the distribution of AI capability scores within cognitive work. The arts and history spend little time on physical steps (10% and 4%, respectively), yet their cognitive steps have low AI capability scores, perhaps because qualitative and interpretive work is less amenable to reinforcement learning. Computer science and statistics, by contrast, have high scores and large AI shares, driven by data analysis, the type of work with the highest AI capability scores across fields.
Fields with a higher use ratio on Claude also tend to have larger AI shares (Figure 14). The AI share is calculated without any Claude use data, so this relationship is further evidence that AI use tracks theoretical AI capability.
Claude use and research time freed up by AI across fields.
The correlation between observed Claude use and the AI share for each field. Each field is a dot, sized by the number of researchers. The vertical axis shows the field’s use ratio on Claude, on a log scale. The horizontal axis shows the estimated share of human research time that could be completed by AI with current capabilities.
Scenarios 2 and 3: Greater automation
In these more speculative scenarios, which depend heavily on assumptions about AI’s reach and costs, greater automation raises both the AI share and the acceleration sharply, and widens the differences between fields.
In Scenario 2, where 75% of non-physical steps can be done by AI, accelerations reach about 8x in computer science, 7x in statistics and library and information science, and 6x in economics. Most other social sciences, mathematics, and physics and astronomy reach 4–5x, while bench and medical sciences reach about 2–3x. The bench sciences and the arts and humanities gain the least, but for different reasons. In the bench sciences, much of the work is physical and must still be done by researchers. In the arts and humanities, the work is mostly cognitive but has low AI capability scores, so few of its steps are among those automated. Automated steps make up 82% of non-physical researcher time in computer science but only 28% in the arts. History, anthropology, and the arts accelerate by about 2x or less.
In Scenario 3, the arts and humanities pull ahead, while the bench sciences remain held back. Once AI automates all non-physical steps, low AI capability scores no longer limit cognitive work, and AI can take on nearly all research work in many fields (Figure 13, left panel). In this speculative scenario, fields with few physical tasks, including statistics, computer science, economics, mathematics, psychology, and most of the social sciences and the arts and humanities, reach about 15–16x. Fields with substantial lab or field work, such as biology, chemistry, materials science, agricultural sciences, and biomedical sciences, reach only 3–4x. Absent automated labs, their physical steps, representing about 40% of researcher time, remain the bottleneck.
Two lessons follow from these scenarios. First, physical bottlenecks remain powerful. Steps that AI cannot perform without physical integrations come to dominate researcher time and budgets, capping acceleration. Second, where no such bottlenecks exist, extraordinary rates of progress become possible, and AI’s cost becomes the limit. Under our assumptions, a task that is fully automated by AI still costs about one-sixteenth of what it would cost a researcher to perform, so accelerations approach about 16x and stop there. Lower AI costs would raise this ceiling proportionately, such that halving the cost of AI, for example, would double the rate of progress. If costs fall sharply, including for harder tasks that AI automates later, the fields without physical bottlenecks could accelerate far beyond these estimates.
These calculations have important limits that cut in both directions. We do not consider constraints at the level of a field rather than a research team. For instance, only so many experiments can run at facilities like the Large Hadron Collider. We also count only the cost of researcher and AI time, not the costs of machinery or inputs for experiments, which can be substantial in the health, physical, and life sciences. Nor do we consider simulations to replace physical experiments, which could ease bottlenecks in some fields. Finally, we do not consider the quality of ideas. If AI identifies better hypotheses with higher chances of success, research could accelerate further; if research taste remains uniquely human, the acceleration would be slower.
Researcher expectations
The scenarios above characterize a range of possibilities. Researchers’ own expectations can provide a unique guide grounded in expertise. To gather their viewpoints, our survey of researchers in the life and health sciences asked when they thought AI, working on its own, would match the best researchers in their field for different categories of research work (Figure 15). Respondents’ expectations are high in the near term: over half expect AI to match top researchers at data analysis by 2027, and 38% say that AI has already reached this level. By 2030, 94% expect AI will match the best researchers in data analysis, 89% in writing, and 72% each in ideation and data gathering. Expectations for ideation and data gathering are lower, consistent with the lower use of Claude for these tasks today.
Expectations for end-to-end AI research without humans in the loop are more conservative, but researchers still expect remarkable progress. About 40% of respondents expect AI to carry out full research projects by 2030, and about 64% by 2035, although 16% say it will never happen. Expectations that AI will autonomously produce scientific breakthroughs are more cautious still, with approximately half of researchers expecting this to occur only after 2035, if ever. Overall, many researchers expect high levels of automation in the next decade, broadly in line with our greater automation scenarios. How fast and to what extent these expectations materialize will depend not only on advances in AI as a software technology, but also on efforts to build automated labs that overcome physical barriers.
Comparing past survey evidence to realized outcomes suggests that AI progress has often been dramatically underestimated (Rosenberg et al. 2026). In a survey in mid-2022, for example, the median estimate for AI achieving gold-level performance in the International Mathematical Olympiad was 2030 among domain experts and 2035 among superforecasters (Karger et al. 2023). AI achieved this milestone in 2025, some five to 10 years ahead of those predictions. While forecasters have systematically underestimated progress in AI capabilities, there are a few exceptions, primarily in domains that require execution in the physical world, such as AI-assisted laboratory tasks in biology.
When researchers expect AI to match the best researchers in their field.
Results come from our own survey. The top four rows correspond to when researchers expect AI, working on its own, to match the best researchers in their field in different task categories. The bottom two rows correspond to when researchers expect AI, without a human scientist in the loop, to go “from question to finding” and to produce “a finding your field would regard as a major advance” in their respective fields.
Discussion
If AI helps speed up scientific discovery, it could contribute to higher standards of living and faster progress in treating disease. Our estimates suggest the potential gains are substantial. But advancements in AI’s research capabilities do not automatically translate into rapid progress; achieving such acceleration will also depend on how we respond to several constraints.
First, adoption can substantially lag capabilities. Diffusion of new technologies is typically slow (Comin and Hobijn 2010), and productivity gains tend to materialize only after organizations restructure around them (David 1990; Brynjolfsson, Rock, and Syverson 2021). Individual learning processes, friction at the organizational or system level, and constraints on AI access or infrastructure can all slow adoption.
Second, research may continue to face bottlenecks that AI does not remove. Physical experimentation, which can be costly and slow, can substantially limit progress even with extremely capable AI. We see this especially in the bench sciences in the scenarios above. Choosing what to study may be another bottleneck. Research questions largely determine a research project’s value, and AI’s capacity to generate good questions remains unclear. If ideation is a bottleneck, it will limit acceleration even as answering a given question becomes much cheaper. Conversely, if AI outstrips humans in formulating high-quality hypotheses, acceleration could be more substantial, especially in domains where testing hypotheses is costly.
Third, AI-enabled research could raise the quantity or quality of research output, with different implications for science. A surge in new research papers could advance a field faster but also overwhelm scientists’ capacity to absorb or verify the results. On the other hand, new technologies, from microscopes and telescopes to statistical software, have historically raised the quality of scientific insights, and AI can likewise make more comprehensive analyses and more ambitious projects feasible. And as papers become easier to produce, the research community may increasingly reward work that is especially novel or high quality. Whether more efficient research leads to greater quantity or greater quality will depend on researchers’ choices and the incentives set by journals, funders, and institutions.
Fourth, the way research is organized may change in ways that are hard to anticipate. As AI becomes more capable and autonomous, AI systems could take the lead in verification, refereeing, and communicating important results, which would ease the absorption problem discussed above. Further in the future, AI research agents might also push the frontiers of science in large communities of their own, independently of humans, using robotics and automated labs. Such autonomous AI research would raise questions about how humans keep track of new knowledge, whether they can understand it, and how it is generated.
Fifth, more autonomous AI systems may increase the challenge of ensuring that AI-driven research remains aligned with human goals. Keeping humans involved in key research decisions, such as which questions to pursue and how to pursue them, may matter for safety and human wellbeing as AI agents become more powerful and creative. Discoveries themselves, or the byproducts of research, can also carry risks, particularly in biology, where the same capabilities that speed up medical advances could also produce dangerous knowledge or materials. In such cases, deliberate checkpoints in the research process may be warranted, requiring us to accept slower progress to reduce risk.
Finally, the work that researchers undertake may change substantially. One effect may be a change in researchers’ job satisfaction. If AI takes over enjoyable or rewarding tasks, satisfaction may fall and fewer people may choose research careers. If AI instead takes over tasks that researchers find tedious, satisfaction may rise. Administrative work is one potential target. In the US, principal investigators on federally funded projects report spending about 44% of their research time meeting administrative requirements rather than doing research (Schneider et al. 2020), and easing this burden could be a large boon, saving time and improving overall satisfaction. Ultimately, the net effect is uncertain and may change as AI’s capabilities evolve. An optimistic view is that AI will expand opportunities for discovery, which is core to what makes research careers rewarding. If science is a voyage into the “endless frontier,” AI may be a new vessel, allowing researchers to travel farther across a vast expanse of research questions and discoveries.
