items.text: bhis-blog published: Core Skills in the Age of AI
items.title: Core Skills in the Age of AI
items.content:
One of the biggest questions I get whenever I’m teaching anything focused on core skills—whether it’s network security, SOC analysis, or ecurity essentials—is whether any of these classes are even necessary anymore because of AI.
The assumption seems to be that AI is going to eliminate the need for foundational knowledge. People believe that AI will simply handle the technical details for us, allowing security professionals to skip over the basics and move directly to the advanced work.
Unfortunately, that assumption creates a sense of hopelessness.
Junior analysts who are trying to enter the field start wondering whether it’s worth studying at all. Companies looking to hire are hesitant because they’re not sure what the workforce will look like in a few years. Everyone is waiting to see where things land.
Context Is Everything
When it comes to core information security skills, I believe we need to recognize something important:
The fundamentals matter more today than they ever have.
The reason is context.
The more context and understanding you have about a technical problem, the more effective AI becomes.
Artificial intelligence is not a replacement for expertise. It amplifies expertise.
If you put AI in the hands of someone who doesn’t understand networking, operating systems, or security fundamentals, the impact is often limited. They may get answers faster, but they have no way to evaluate whether those answers are correct.
Put the same tools in the hands of someone who understands TCP/IP, operating systems, network architecture, authentication, and how systems actually work, and AI becomes an incredible force multiplier.
As we move into the future, it will become even more important for security professionals to understand the basics. Those foundational skills provide the context necessary to ask better questions, recognize bad answers, and effectively leverage increasingly powerful AI tools.
What Chess Can Teach Us
I also think we can look at chess as a preview of where our industry is heading.
Chess is more popular today than it has ever been. There are more strong chess players than at any other point in history. At the same time, AI engines can defeat even the world’s best players without breaking a sweat.
So why hasn’t AI killed chess?
Because the chess community embraced it.
Players use AI engines like Stockfish to analyze games, identify mistakes, study openings, improve endgame strategy, and accelerate learning. Tournament organizers use AI to help detect cheating. Coaches use AI to provide insights that would have been impossible to deliver at scale just a few decades ago.
The result isn’t fewer chess players. In fact, it is the opposite. The other result is better chess players.
Where Cybersecurity Is Heading
I believe cybersecurity is heading down a very similar path.
AI will help us learn faster. It will help us identify patterns more quickly. It will help us automate repetitive work and explore technical problems at a scale that wasn’t previously possible.
But none of that eliminates the need for foundational knowledge.
In fact, it increases its importance.
The people who understand the fundamentals will be the ones who get the most value from AI. They’ll be able to guide it, challenge it, verify it, and use it to solve increasingly complex problems.
The future of cybersecurity isn’t humans versus AI.
It’s humans with strong fundamentals using AI to become dramatically more effective than ever before.

antisyphontraining.com/instructor/john-strand/

items.title: DigDug: Making Your Payload Too Big to Scan
items.content:
by Jason Downey
If you spend any amount of time as a pentester, you learn pretty quickly that evading AV and EDR is not a one-time problem. It is a constant, ongoing arms race. You find something that works, it gets signatured, and you are back to the drawing board. Every engagement is a fresh puzzle, and your toolbox needs to have more than one trick in it. DigDug is one of those tricks that is almost too simple to believe, but it works.
Some AV and EDR engines will not analyze files above a certain size threshold. The exact size varies by vendor, but conversations across offensive security Slack channels and Twitter posts put it somewhere around 100-150MB. Nobody has published a definitive list of thresholds per vendor, at least that I have found, but the pattern is consistent enough that the technique has become a staple in our evasion playbook at Red Siege. DigDug exploits that behavior by inflating your executable to whatever size you need.
More Than Just Padding
What makes DigDug different from slapping null bytes onto the end of a binary is how it inflates the file. It appends words from a dictionary. This matters because vendors like CrowdStrike Falcon measure entropy as part of their analysis. Random data (high entropy/randomness) and null byte padding both produce patterns often used as detection by AV/EDR. A binary stuffed with dictionary words? In the eyes of AV/EDR looks a lot more like a legitimate application with embedded string resources.
By default, DigDug ships with a modified version of the Google 10,000 English dictionary. There is also an included dictionary built from strings extracted from executables in Windows System32, which blends in even more naturally on a Windows target. You can supply your own dictionary too. Want your padding in French? Allez-y (go for it).
Steal a Signature While You Are At It
DigDug also integrates SigThief, which copies the digital signature from a legitimate executable onto your inflated binary. Pair the inflated file size with a stolen signature from something like consent.exe, and you have got a payload that looks a lot more trustworthy to automated analysis.
python3 digdug.py -i payload.exe -m 150 -d dictionaries/google-10000-english-usa-gt5.txt -s consent.exe
That one command inflates your payload to 150MB with English word padding and a signature lifted from a trusted Windows binary.
The Ongoing Game
I have been on engagements where our initial payload gets flagged within minutes of landing on disk. EDR picks it up, quarantines it, and now you are burned. The client security team is alerted, and you need a different approach, fast. Techniques like file size inflation are not glamorous and they will not make for an exciting conference talk, but they are the kind of practical, low-effort adjustments that keep you moving forward when your primary tooling gets caught.
The reality is that no single evasion technique works forever. What works is having a deep bench of options and knowing when to reach for each one. DigDug is a quick play. Five seconds of effort, and suddenly your payload is big enough that a lot of engines just skip over. That is a good trade off when it comes to time and potential upside, especially when you can pair it with other evasion techniques.
For Defenders
If you are on a blue team, this should raise a question… does your AV/EDR actually analyze large files? If there is a file size ceiling on your static analysis, attackers will find it and exploit it. Test your tools with oversized binaries and make sure you are not giving attackers a free pass just because a file is bigger than some arbitrary threshold. Also be aware of where you have big files on the network and test to make sure it isn’t placing an excessive burden on your end points. It’s a balancing act.
DigDug takes its name from the arcade classic where the whole point of the game was inflating your enemies until they burst. Honestly, it’s a perfect metaphor. (Yes, I just gave a public compliment to Mike Saunders.) We’re inflating binaries until AV gives up trying to analyze them. The only difference is nobody’s putting quarters into this machine, and the high score is measured in high fives shared over bypassed detections. Sometimes the simplest tricks are the most effective.
DigDug is free on the
Red Siege GitHub
.
About Jason Downey, Senior Security Consultant
Jason Downey has ten years of information security experience, including multiple years of consultant penetration testing for organizations of all sizes. He started his career
in network and systems administration, which means he learned how networks are built before he started getting paid to break into them. Jason is best known for his vishing
and social engineering expertise, where a friendly voice and a solid pretext have opened more doors than any exploit. He also specializes in network penetration testing and
physical security assessments. Jason has spoken to audiences ranging from youth initiatives to major security conferences, has helped author training courses, creates content
for SiegeCasts, and spends his free time helping newcomers find their way into the industry.
Certifications:
CRTO, GPEN, GCIH, CCNA R&S, CCNA Security, CEH, CHFI

items.text: xlab-qianxin published: CWPdoor: The Invisible Backdoor Living Inside Control Web Panel
items.title: CWPdoor: The Invisible Backdoor Living Inside Control Web Panel
items.content:
Background
On June 29, 2026, the
XLab's Cyber Threat Insight and Analysis System(CTIA)
captured a suspicious script named
cwpsrv_update.sh
. The script downloads a file named
cwpsrv
from the remote server
136.0.141.71
and replaces the file of the same name on the system. Our analysis confirmed that the downloaded
cwpsrv
is a passive backdoor that can be triggered by specific headers in HTTP/HTTPS traffic to remotely execute commands specified by the attacker. Since it targets Control Web Panel, we named it
cwpdoor
.
cwpdoor is not standalone malware. Instead, it is embedded in cwpsrv—
the attacker inserts malicious code into the cwpsrv source code and recompiles it
. As a passive backdoor, it exhibits no obvious malicious behavior during normal operation and behaves just like a legitimate cwpsrv server. Its backdoor logic is triggered only when it receives a specially crafted request from the attacker. At the same time, it suppresses logging for that request, leaving no trace of the interaction in the access logs.
This combination of directly replacing the legitimate cwpsrv binary, passive triggering, and log suppression makes cwpdoor exceptionally stealthy.
Control Web Panel (CWP) is a free, open-source server management control panel for CentOS and other Linux distributions. It provides a graphical interface for managing server resources such as websites, DNS, and email, eliminating the need for cumbersome SSH command-line operations. cwpsrv, meanwhile, is the web server dedicated to CWP's own management panel. It is responsible for serving the CWP control panel interface and its related built-in applications. According to data from
QiAnXin's Hunter Platform
, more than
340,000
CWP instances were exposed to the internet over the past month, making all of them potential targets for cwpdoor infection.
On September 30, 2026, a file named
evidencia.tgz
was uploaded to VirusTotal from Brazil. The archive contained two malicious files:
libkeyutils.so.1.5.2
and
cwpsrv.suspeito
. Most security vendors correctly identified
libkeyutils
as the Ebury backdoor, but the detection rate for
cwpsrv.suspeito
was zero. That file is the cwpdoor backdoor. This indicates that the campaign was not merely experimental:
real victims already exist in the wild
. (Note: The relationship between Ebury and cwpdoor remains unclear. It is possible that the two malware families were implanted on the same server by different attackers.)
Since mainstream security vendors have not yet identified cwpdoor, we decided to publish this article to share the relevant intelligence with the security community. We also welcome leads from industry peers with unique visibility into this activity, in the hope of clarifying cwpdoor's distribution channels and working together to improve cybersecurity.
Script Analysis
The basic information about the infection script captured on June 29, 2026, is shown below:
MD5: e505d4ffa21cf494a5dc2d7c8f4f1236
Magic: Bourne-Again shell script text executable
Name: cwpsrv_update.sh
The script's functionality is straightforward. Disguised as a "version update," it is a cwpsrv replacement and deployment tool (supporting only versions 1.24.0 and 1.15.10). It must run with root privileges. First, it checks the local cwpsrv version, downloads the corresponding binary, and verifies that the version matches. It then backs up the original file, stops the cwpsrv service, overwrites
/usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv
with the malicious binary, restarts the service, and checks whether the master, worker, and helper processes are running. If the health check fails, it automatically rolls back; if it succeeds, it deletes the temporary files and backup. Most notably, whether the operation succeeds or fails, the script restores the new binary's atime/mtime and its parent directory's timestamp to their original values. It also runs
history -d
to delete the current session's command history. As a result, under routine checks such as
ls
and
stat
, the replaced file appears as though it has "never been modified." The script also reports the update result back to
136.0.141.71
.
cwpdoor Analysis
We captured two cwpdoor samples, targeting cwpsrv versions 1.15.10 and 1.24.0, respectively. The following analysis focuses primarily on the sample targeting version 1.15.10. Its basic information is as follows:
MD5: 965aea67fb40de1bab5169ada993349f
Magic: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked (uses shared libs), for GNU/Linux 2.6.32, stripped
Name:cwpsrv_1.15.10
In essence, cwpsrv is a customized server based on Nginx by CWP. It is specifically responsible for serving the CWP control panel interface and related built-in applications. The cwpdoor deployed in this attack adds malicious backdoor functionality to the cwpsrv source code. The backdoor can be triggered by specific HTTP traffic to remotely execute commands issued by the attacker.
A complete attack interaction proceeds as follows:
Initiation:
The attacker crafts an HTTP request containing the following headers:
X-Ngx-Integrity-Time
(timestamp),
X-Ngx-Integrity-Data
(AES-encrypted command), and
X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig
(RSA signature).
Verification:
The cwpdoor master process intercepts the request at the entry point, validates the timestamp, and verifies the signature using its embedded public key. If either check fails, the request continues to be processed as ordinary traffic, and the backdoor logic is not triggered.
Execution:
Once verification succeeds, the master process decrypts the command and passes it to a helper child process through a Unix domain socket for execution.
Response:
The execution result is encrypted with AES and returned to the attacker in an HTTP 200 response with the content type
application/octet-stream
. The request is also excluded from logging.
Although the cwpdoor sample has been stripped, it still retains many symbols, including function names, making reverse engineering relatively straightforward. The following sections briefly examine how the backdoor works and summarize the indicators of infection on a compromised host, helping system administrators and incident responders quickly investigate and remediate infections.
① Indicators of Infection
cwpdoor is not standalone malware; its malicious code is embedded in the legitimate cwpsrv server. One way to determine whether a host is infected is to look for the Unix domain socket
ngx_http_integrity_helper
, which cwpdoor uses for inter-process communication. Run the following command for a quick check:
ss -axp | grep integrity
.
In addition to the socket, there are indicators at the process and file levels:
Process indicator:
Run
ps aux | grep cwpsrv
and check whether the output shows any suspicious helper child processes associated with cwpsrv.
File indicator:
Run
strings /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv | grep X-Ngx-Integrity
and check whether any suspicious strings are present.
② Stealthy Backdoor Channel
cwpdoor adds two functions,
ngx_http_integrity_init
and
ngx_http_integrity_check
, to implement its passive backdoor functionality.
ngx_http_integrity_init
(initializer / implantation point)
This function is called at the end of the
ngx_http_block
configuration-parsing stage. Its purpose is to implant a persistent backdoor service in the cwpsrv process. It first iterates through
ngx_modules
to locate and cache the index of the logging module for subsequent log suppression. It then cleans up any potentially lingering helper processes, creates and binds the Unix domain socket
ngx_http_integrity_helper
, and spawns a separate helper child process to execute commands issued by the attacker.
ngx_http_integrity_check
(trigger / command channel)
This function is called at the entry point of
ngx_http_process_request
, serving as the external trigger for the backdoor. It extracts
X-Ngx-Integrity-Time
,
X-Ngx-Integrity-Data
, and
X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig
from the HTTP request headers.
The
X-Ngx-Integrity-Time
field carries a timestamp. cwpdoor validates it against a time window of ±300 seconds.
The
X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig
field contains a Base64-encoded digital signature, which cwpdoor verifies using its embedded RSA public key. The signed data is the concatenation of
<X-Ngx-Integrity-Time value>:<X-Ngx-Integrity-Data value>
. Therefore, changing either the timestamp or the ciphertext independently invalidates the signature. By binding the three fields together and enforcing a ±300-second time window, the mechanism
provides replay protection and authorization control
.
The RSA public key embedded in the sample is XOR-encrypted. It can be recovered by XORing each byte with
0x55
.
The decrypted public key is shown below:
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEAwf9x0uLMxBK0AaCJuBsD
cqZgCasvDlgoA5NgPKPJrFP4YdoAztt6EAlZl/jC9LrbVAlmuXD9pt4tQkZAiiZ3
ia0I4nDzB+iLtYR2DjSwsjMSD5x2gNRdew5J1gflVVk1gub3izisExyxnZL0ahgM
4kszCeBS6ZijbzH3dZJvANdTnWulxL+rFsjm1RGrIv0B8bD8zAMxuC1NRvwM2x/u
7nhqrMaG4qHHoCEA4JTags56I03xBpHpH+jqj+Ps8CRkHCvwSeqZN2UgaP1nduLj
xMnAuffjHHErcJI4INI8CM3+SKdB0ulxPYRWHc6c4+ZO5w55noEoZ1f7Xd1YFWPW
jQIDAQAB
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----
The
X-Ngx-Integrity-Data
field contains the AES-encrypted attack command encoded in Base64. After Base64 decoding, the first 16 bytes are the IV, and the remaining bytes are the AES-256-CBC ciphertext. The AES key is derived from the SHA-256 digest of the embedded RSA public key string.
The decrypted command is sent to the helper process through the Unix domain socket for execution. The execution result is also encrypted with AES and returned in an HTTP 200 response with the content type
application/octet-stream
, forming a covert, bidirectionally encrypted command channel.
When a request triggers the backdoor, it copies and tampers with that request's module context array, replacing the context pointer corresponding to the logging module. This prevents the request from being logged normally, breaking the forensic trail. Combined with cwpdoor's
zero detection rate
, these techniques form a complete, stealthy attack cycle that is
"hidden from view and absent from the logs."
Conclusion
This is all the intelligence we currently have on cwpdoor. Network administrators can investigate their systems using the indicators described in the preceding "Indicators of Infection" section. If an infection is confirmed, we recommend taking the following steps:
Locate the legitimate backup file created by the attacker in
/usr/local/cwpsrv/bin
(with the naming format
cwpsrv.prev-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
) and use it to replace the malicious
cwpsrv
;
Upgrade to the latest version and confirm that
ss -axp | grep integrity
no longer returns a match;
Immediately rotate all control panel credentials. Since the backdoor can execute arbitrary commands, these credentials should be considered compromised. We recommend treating the host as compromised and investigating it for other threats.
We do not yet know which vulnerability cwpdoor uses to spread, nor can we determine whether Ebury in
evidencia.tgz
is related to cwpdoor. We welcome industry peers with unique visibility into this activity, as well as readers with relevant inside knowledge, to share additional intelligence. If you are interested in our research or would like assistance, please contact us via
X
.
IOC
SAMPLE MD5
e505d4ffa21cf494a5dc2d7c8f4f1236 script
965aea67fb40de1bab5169ada993349f *cwpsrv_1.15.10
d3f4e95113d49ab3991b45e457bda75b *cwpsrv_1.24.0
Downloader URL
http://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_update.sh
http://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.15.10
http://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.24.0
Downloader IP
136.0.141.71

items.title: 警惕 cwpdoor：寄生在 Control Web Panel 中的零检出被动后门
items.content:
背景介绍
2026年6月29日，
XLab大网威胁感知系统
捕获了一个名为“cwpsrv_update.sh”的可疑脚本。该脚本的功能是从远程服务器136.0.141.71下载cwpsrv文件，并替换系统中的同名文件。经分析确认，下载的cwpsrv是一个被动后门，可通过HTTP/HTTPS流量中特定的header触发，远程执行攻击者指定的命令。鉴于其针对的是Control Web Panel，我们将其命名为cwpdoor。
cwpdoor 并非独立的恶意软件，而是寄生于 cwpsrv——
攻击者在 cwpsrv 源码中植入恶意代码后重新编译而成
。作为被动式后门，它在运行时并无明显恶意行为，表现如同正常的 cwpsrv 服务器；只有接收到攻击者构造的特定请求时，才会被动触发后门逻辑。而在触发的同时，它还会抑制本次请求的日志记录，使这次交互在访问日志中不留痕迹。
这种"直接替换正常 cwpsrv 二进制文件"配合"被动触发"再叠加"日志抑制"的技术组合，极大增强了 cwpdoor 的隐蔽性
。
Control Web Panel（CWP）是一款面向CentOS等Linux发行版的免费开源服务器管理控制面板，用于通过图形界面管理网站、DNS、邮箱等服务器资源，替代繁琐的SSH命令行操作；而cwpsrv则是CWP自身管理面板专用的Web服务器，专门负责运行CWP的控制面板界面及相关内置应用。根据
奇安信网络空间测绘全球鹰图平台
的数据，过去一个月暴露在互联网的 CWP 实例超过 34 万，它们都是cwpdoor的潜在感染目标。
2026年9月30日，一个名为evidencia.tgz的文件从巴西上传至VirusTotal，该压缩包内含俩个恶意文件：libkeyutils.so.1.5.2和cwpsrv.suspeito。其中libkeyutils已被大多数厂商正确判定为Ebury后门，但cwpsrv.suspeito的检测率为0——该文件正是cwpdoor后门。这表明此次攻击活动并非实验性质，
在野已存在真实受害者
。（注：Ebury 与 cwpdoor 的关系尚不明确，有可能是同一台服务器被不同攻击者植入的两种恶意软件。）
考虑到主流安全厂商尚未识别cwpdoor，我们决定撰写本文，向安全社区分享相关情报。我们也希望有独特视野的友商不吝分享线索，以厘清cwpdoor的传播渠道，共同维护网络安全。
脚本分析
2026年6月29日捕获的感染脚本的基本信息如下所示：
MD5: e505d4ffa21cf494a5dc2d7c8f4f1236
Magic: Bourne-Again shell script text executable
Name: cwpsrv_update.sh
这个脚本的功能非常直观，它是一个以“版本更新”为伪装的 cwpsrv 替换投放器（仅支持 1.24.0 和 1.15.10 两个版本）：它必须以root 权限运行，先检测本地 cwpsrv 版本，下载对应二进制并校验版本一致后，备份原文件、停止 cwpsrv 服务、用恶意二进制覆盖 /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv，再启动服务并检查 master/worker/helper 进程是否存活；若健康检查失败则自动回滚，若成功则删除临时文件和备份。最关键的是，它在成功或失败后都会把新二进制的 atime/mtime 以及所在目录的时间戳恢复成原文件的旧时间，并执行 history -d 删除当前会话命令历史，使替换后的文件在 ls、stat 等常规检查下看起来“从未被改动”，同时向 136.0.141.71 回传更新结果。
cwpdoor分析
我们共捕获了2个cwpdoor样本，分别针对cwpsrv 1.15.10和1.24.0两个版本。下文以针对1.15.10的样本为主要分析对象，其基本信息如下：
MD5: 965aea67fb40de1bab5169ada993349f
Magic: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), dynamically linked (uses shared libs), for GNU/Linux 2.6.32, stripped
Name:cwpsrv_1.15.10
cwpsrv本质上是CWP基于Nginx定制的服务器，专门负责运行CWP的控制面板界面及相关内置应用。此次攻击中投放的cwpdoor，是在cwpsrv源码基础上加入了恶意后门功能——后门可通过特定的HTTP流量触发，远程执行攻击者下发的指令。
一次完整的攻击交互如下所示：
发起：攻击者构造 HTTP 请求，在头部携带 X-Ngx-Integrity-Time（时间戳）、X-Ngx-Integrity-Data（AES 加密的指令）、X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig（RSA 签名）。
校验：cwpdoor 主进程在请求入口拦截，校验时间戳并用内置公钥验签；任一不通过，请求即按普通流量继续处理，不触发后门逻辑。
执行：校验通过后，主进程解密出指令，经 Unix 套接字交给 helper 子进程执行。
回传：执行结果经 AES 加密，以 application/octet-stream 的 200 响应回传攻击者，同时抑制本次请求的日志记录。
cwpdoor 样本虽经 strip 处理，但仍保留了大量函数名等符号，逆向分析门槛很低。下文将简要剖析后门功能的实现方式，并梳理主机被感染后的特征，以帮助运维和应急人员快速排查与处置。
①感染后的特征
cwpdoor 并非独立的恶意软件，其恶意代码寄生于正常的 cwpsrv 服务器中。判断是否被感染，可依据 cwpdoor 依赖 Unix 域套接字
ngx_http_integrity_helper
进行消息传递这一特征，通过执行
ss -axp | grep integrity
进行快速排查。
除套接字外，进程与文件层面也有特征可查：
进程特征：ps aux | grep cwpsrv，检查输出中cwpsrv是否存在异常的 helper 子进程。
文件特征：strings /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv | grep X-Ngx-Integrity，检查输出中是否存在异常字串。
②隐蔽的后门信道
cwpdoor 新增了 ngx_http_integrity_init 和 ngx_http_integrity_check 两个函数，用于实现被动后门功能。
ngx_http_integrity_init（启动器 / 植入点）
该函数在 ngx_http_block 配置解析收尾阶段被调用，作用是在 cwpsrv进程中植入一个常驻后门服务。它首先遍历 ngx_modules 定位并缓存日志模块索引（供后续日志抑制使用），随后清理可能残留的旧 helper 进程，创建并绑定 Unix 域套接字 ngx_http_integrity_helper，并创建一个独立的 helper 子进程，用于执行攻击者下发的指令。
ngx_http_integrity_check（触发器 / 指令通道）
该函数在 ngx_http_process_request 入口处被调用，构成后门的外部触发点。它从 HTTP 请求头中提取 X-Ngx-Integrity-Time、X-Ngx-Integrity-Data 和 X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig。
其中
X-Ngx-Integrity-Time
字段携带时间戳，cwpdoor 以 ±300 秒的时间窗口进行校验。
X-Ngx-Integrity-Sig
字段承载 Base64 编码的数字签名，cwpdoor 用内置 RSA 公钥对其验签。验签原文是
<X-Ngx-Integrity-Time 的值>:<X-Ngx-Integrity-Data 的值>
拼成的整体，因此单独改动时间戳或密文都会导致签名失效——三者被绑定在一起，再配合 ±300 秒的时间窗口，
共同实现防重放与授权控制
。
样本内置RSA公钥采用XOR加密，解密时只需将每个字节与0x55异或即可还原。
解密后的公钥如下所示：
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEAwf9x0uLMxBK0AaCJuBsD
cqZgCasvDlgoA5NgPKPJrFP4YdoAztt6EAlZl/jC9LrbVAlmuXD9pt4tQkZAiiZ3
ia0I4nDzB+iLtYR2DjSwsjMSD5x2gNRdew5J1gflVVk1gub3izisExyxnZL0ahgM
4kszCeBS6ZijbzH3dZJvANdTnWulxL+rFsjm1RGrIv0B8bD8zAMxuC1NRvwM2x/u
7nhqrMaG4qHHoCEA4JTags56I03xBpHpH+jqj+Ps8CRkHCvwSeqZN2UgaP1nduLj
xMnAuffjHHErcJI4INI8CM3+SKdB0ulxPYRWHc6c4+ZO5w55noEoZ1f7Xd1YFWPW
jQIDAQAB
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----
X-Ngx-Integrity-Data
字段为 Base64 编码的 AES 加密攻击指令：Base64 解码后，前 16 字节是 IV，其余为 AES-256-CBC 密文；AES 密钥则由内置 RSA 公钥字符串的 SHA256 摘要派生。
解密后的指令经 Unix 套接字送入 helper进程 执行，执行结果同样以 AES 加密，并封装为 application/octet-stream 的 200 响应回传，由此构成双向加密的隐蔽指令通道。
后门一旦命中触发请求，便会复制该请求的模块上下文数组并加以篡改，将日志模块对应的上下文指针替换，使本次请求无法正常写入日志、溯源链就此断裂。再叠加 cwpdoor 的"零查杀"，二者共同
构成"藏得住、查不到"的完整无痕攻击闭环
。
总结
这是我们目前掌握的关于 cwpdoor 的全部情报。网络管理员可依据前文「感染后的特征」章节进行排查。若确认已被感染，建议按以下步骤处置：
在 /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin 目录下找到攻击者备份的正常文件（命名格式 cwpsrv.prev-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)），用其替换恶意的 cwpsrv；
升级至最新版本，并确认 ss -axp | grep integrity 不再命中；
立即轮换所有面板凭据，由于后门可执行任意命令，相关凭据应视为已泄露，建议按主机已失陷排查同机其他威胁。
我们尚不清楚 cwpdoor 通过何种漏洞传播，也不确定 evidencia.tgz 中的 Ebury 与 cwpdoor 是否存在关联。欢迎有独特视野的友商、了解内幕的读者向我们提供更多情报。如果你对我们的研究感兴趣，或希望获取帮助，可通过
X 平台
与我们联系。

items.target: Vulnerability Analysis: CVE-2026-109518 APT MitM Vulnerability Grants Root Access
items.text: denizhalil-blogs published: Vulnerability Analysis: CVE-2026-109518 APT MitM Vulnerability Grants Root Access
items.title: Vulnerability Analysis: CVE-2026-109518 APT MitM Vulnerability Grants Root Access
items.content:
Introduction
Package managers are the backbone of system maintenance and software deployment in Linux environments. A critical security flaw, designated as CVE-2026-109518, has been identified in APT, the default package manager for Debian and Ubuntu distributions. Discovered by security researcher Max Justicz, this vulnerability allows a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacker to intercept package downloads, bypass verification, and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. Because APT is ubiquitous across Debian-based systems, understanding and mitigating this threat is an immediate priority for system administrators and security professionals. As organizations increasingly rely on automated infrastructure and continuous integration pipelines, the integrity of these core utilities is paramount. The discovery of this flaw highlights a significant blind spot in how legacy fetching mechanisms interact with modern threat landscapes. When a foundational tool like APT is compromised, the entire security posture of the server fleet collapses, making rapid patching and threat awareness absolutely essential to maintaining operational continuity and data integrity.
Learning Objectives
Understand the fundamental mechanism of CVE-2026-109518 and how it compromises the package installation process.
Identify the specific configuration settings, such as
Acquire::Retries
, that enable the exploit.
Recognize the specific Linux distributions and APT versions vulnerable to this attack.
Grasp the operational steps required to remediate the vulnerability across enterprise environments.
What is APT MitM vulnerability grants root access (CVE-2026-109518)
CVE-2026-109518 is a critical security flaw with a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.7, specifically targeting the Advanced Package Tool (APT) used heavily in Debian and Ubuntu ecosystems. It fundamentally breaks the trust model between the local operating system and remote package repositories. The core issue lies in how APT processes failed HTTP requests and manages its subsequent retry attempts when downloading software updates or new installations. To exploit this vulnerability, a malicious actor must first establish a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) position on the network. This means the attacker is strategically situated between the target Linux machine and the upstream Debian or Ubuntu package server. From this vantage point, the attacker can observe, intercept, and modify the unencrypted HTTP traffic flowing to the package manager, setting the stage for payload injection. Once the attacker successfully manipulates the connection state, they can swap a cryptographically verified package with a malicious alternative during the automated retry phase. Because APT operations inherently require superuser privileges to install software, modify system directories, and execute deployment scripts, the injected malicious code is automatically executed with root access. This grants the attacker complete, unfettered control over the compromised machine.
CVSS 4.0 Score:
7.7 (High Priority), reflecting the severe impact of local network root-level compromise.
Attack Vector:
Network-based Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) manipulation of unencrypted HTTP traffic.
Trigger Mechanism:
Exploitation of the
Acquire::Retries
configuration during simulated or real failed package downloads.
Final Impact:
Arbitrary code execution as the root user, leading to immediate and full system takeover.
[ Target Machine (APT) ]
|
| 1. HTTP GET /legitimate-package.deb
v
[ MitM Attacker ] --(Drops/Redirects request)--> [ Legitimate Repo ]
|
| 2. HTTP 500 / Redirect Error (Forces APT to Retry)
v
[ Target Machine (APT) ]
|
| 3. Retries Download (Acquire::Retries triggered)
v
[ MitM Attacker ] --(Injects Malicious .deb file)
|
| 4. Malicious Package Received & Executed as Root
v
[ System Compromised ]
Technical Detail: How the Vulnerability Works
The technical execution of CVE-2026-109518 is an elegant abuse of a standard reliability feature. Under normal circumstances, if APT encounters a network hiccup or a temporary server error, it relies on the
Acquire::Retries
directive to re-establish the connection and attempt the download again. This is intended to prevent broken installations on unstable networks. However, the core flaw exists because the developers failed to enforce strict cryptographic state verification consistently across these subsequent retry attempts over HTTP. An attacker actively monitoring the network traffic waits for an
apt-get install
or
apt update
command to be initiated by the victim. When the system requests a package, the attacker intercepts the HTTP traffic and intentionally responds with specific HTTP status codes, such as temporary redirects (3xx) or server errors (5xx). This artificial disruption forces APT to drop the initial, secure transaction flow and immediately fall back to its retry routine.
It is exactly during this narrow window of the retry phase that the exploit occurs. The MitM attacker intercepts the retried HTTP request and serves a heavily modified
.deb
package in place of the requested software. Because the validation checks are bypassed or improperly handled during the forced HTTP redirect sequence, APT accepts the fraudulent package. The pre-install (
preinst
) or post-install (
postinst
) scripts embedded within the malicious
.deb
file are then executed natively by the system as root.
Traffic Interception:
The attacker monitors port 80 to catch outbound APT HTTP requests.
Error Injection:
The attacker serves specific HTTP 503 or 302 responses to disrupt the initial download state.
Retry Trigger:
APT automatically initiates a new request based on the vulnerable
Acquire::Retries
logic.
Payload Execution:
The malicious
.deb
is unpacked, and its scripts run with maximum system permissions.
Affected Software & Plugins
The scope of CVE-2026-109518 is extensive, affecting a vast ecosystem of Debian and Ubuntu-based distributions deployed across enterprise servers, cloud environments, and personal workstations. The vulnerability’s presence is primarily dictated by the default network configuration shipped with the operating system. Because package managers are fundamental components, any downstream distribution (like Linux Mint or Pop!_OS) that relies on the main APT repositories and standard configurations inherits this vulnerability. The critical differentiator between a vulnerable and secure system out-of-the-box is the
Acquire::Retries
setting. Modern distributions have this feature enabled by default to improve user experience on unstable connections, inadvertently opening the door to this exploit. Conversely, older legacy systems are technically immune under their factory settings, but frequently become vulnerable because administrators often enable the retry feature manually to stabilize automated deployment scripts and continuous integration pipelines.
Debian 12 (Bookworm):
Vulnerable by default due to standard retry configurations.
Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS & 26.04 LTS:
Vulnerable by default; patched builds are actively being distributed to security archives.
Debian 11 & Ubuntu 20.04 LTS:
Not vulnerable by default, but highly exposed if
Acquire::Retries
is manually configured by users or scripts.
Ubuntu 14.04 (via Ubuntu Pro):
Affected under specific retry configurations, but currently receiving patched versions through Extended Security Maintenance.
Conclusion
CVE-2026-109518 serves as a stark reminder that even the most trusted, foundational utilities in an operating system can harbor critical security flaws. The APT package manager has been a reliable cornerstone for Linux administrators for decades, but this vulnerability demonstrates how features designed for reliability—like automated HTTP retries—can be weaponized by a sophisticated Man-in-the-Middle attacker. It highlights the inherent risks of relying on unencrypted HTTP traffic for system-level software distribution, even when cryptographic package signing mechanisms are assumed to be in place. While there are currently no reported instances of this vulnerability being actively exploited in the wild, the detailed public disclosure provides threat actors with a clear blueprint for attack. Local network adversaries, malicious Wi-Fi hotspots, or compromised proxy servers could leverage this flaw to silently hijack enterprise servers or personal workstations during routine updates. The ease with which root access is achieved makes this a highly attractive vector for initial access and lateral movement within corporate networks. Immediate remediation is non-negotiable for anyone managing Debian or Ubuntu infrastructure. System administrators must prioritize patching APT to the latest secure versions provided by their respective distribution maintainers. Until patches can be fully validated and deployed, security teams should actively audit their configurations to determine if
Acquire::Retries
is needlessly enabled on older systems, and enforce strict network monitoring to detect anomalous HTTP redirect behaviors aimed at package repositories.
What is a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Attack?
Updating Kali Linux: A Step-by-Step Guide
What is an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)?
APT and APT-GET in Linux Package Management Cheat Sheet
Debian vs Ubuntu: Which Linux Distribution is Suitable for You?
The post
Vulnerability Analysis: CVE-2026-109518 APT MitM Vulnerability Grants Root Access
appeared first on
DenizHalil - Professional Cybersecurity Consulting and Penetration Testing
.

items.target: 十个月，给 LobeHub 换掉 Ant Design：向 Base UI 与 StyleX 的渐进式迁移
items.text: innei published: 十个月，给 LobeHub 换掉 Ant Design：向 Base UI 与 StyleX 的渐进式迁移
items.title: 十个月，给 LobeHub 换掉 Ant Design：向 Base UI 与 StyleX 的渐进式迁移
items.content:
The starting point: a performance tuning pass
During my first month at LobeHub, I ran a performance optimization pass, documented with benchmarks in
"Performance and DX Optimizations at LobeHub"
. The heaviest bottlenecks in that pass were all style-related: CSS-in-JS Flexbox components like react-layout-kit numbered in the hundreds on a single page, each generating CSS; the
useStyle
running across almost every component recalculated styles on every re-render; and a single antd Tooltip took 0.5ms on its own. The first two could be fixed by switching styling solutions, but Tooltip required a full rewrite. I rebuilt both it and Popover with Base UI—the first time Base UI was used in lobe-ui.
With those fixes in place, the remaining overhead came from antd components themselves. Since antd's UI was also notoriously hard to customize deeply, replacing it was the obvious next move. I had wanted to do this for a while, but never started because manually rewriting a codebase of this size was unrealistic, and AI wasn't capable enough yet.
When we actually started, this was what we were facing:
@lobehub/ui
had almost a hundred component modules, with behavior tightly coupled to antd and all component styles written in Emotion-based
antd-style
, which generated CSS at runtime and injected it into the document on every page load. Downstream, five ecosystem libraries—icons, editor, charts, tts, and fluent-emoji—declared it as a peer dependency, and at the top layer, hundreds of business files in lobe-chat directly imported from
import ... from 'antd'
. Meanwhile, product features shipped weekly, so maintaining a long-running rewrite branch wasn't an option. The entire migration had to happen without interrupting delivery, split into two parallel tracks: first swap out the underlying component foundation from antd to Base UI, then switch styling from runtime Emotion to compile-time StyleX.
Letting old and new components coexist in the same package
lobe-ui#448
rewrote Tooltip. Beyond performance gains, it also resolved seven Linear issues: positioning drift, tooltips failing to dismiss, and elements snapping back to (0, 0) when their host unmounted. Base UI is headless, providing only behavior and accessibility while leaving DOM structure and styling to us, so we could customize everything freely without fighting antd's limitations.
The next question was how to make the transition. With weekly product releases and several downstream libraries tracking our changes, ripping out antd all at once wasn't practical. Instead, I opted for coexistence: build new components with Base UI, package them alongside the antd versions, and migrate product call sites one component at a time. Throughout January 2026, we gradually added
lobe-ui#444
's Base UI Menu–based DropdownMenu and ContextMenu, alongside LobeSwitch and LobeSelect. To avoid name clashes with their antd counterparts, they initially carried a Lobe prefix or a V2 suffix.
On March 2,
lobe-ui#467
released v5, formalizing this coexistence in the package structure: adding a
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
subpath where LobeSelect and LobeSwitch were moved (dropping their prefixes), while DropdownMenu, Toast, ContextMenu, and ScrollArea were exported from there as well. The package itself also became ESM-only. Subsequent components followed the exact same pattern: the implementation lived under
src/base-ui/
, while the root entry only re-exported it. For instance, when
lobe-ui#486
migrated Popover,
@lobehub/ui
and
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
were both valid, requiring zero changes in product code. From here on, migrating a component took just two steps: write the new implementation under base-ui, then switch the call sites in product code.
Components had to be drop-in replacements, locked down with linting once migrated
Between March and September, components were ported into base-ui roughly in this order: overlays, basic controls, forms, display, and layout.
Overlays first
This came down to two reasons. To begin with, overlays naturally belong together: Dropdown, Popover, Tooltip, Modal, and Drawer all share floating positioning and stacking management, making them ideal to tackle together. Later,
lobe-ui#518
unified their z-index management under a single layer manager. The second reason was how Modal was structured. Antd's Modal is primarily declarative, requiring components to be mounted on the React tree in advance:
open
is
false
, its children still render, re-rendering whenever ancestor state updates. With multiple Modals on a page, that overhead adds up on every single render. An imperative Modal creates an instance only when invoked and destroys it when closed, shifting the cost to the user action that opens it. I previously wrote about this in
"Why I Recommend Imperative Modals,"
and base-ui's Modal has supported both imperative and declarative patterns since its
first release
.
In the top example, every closed Modal participates in every render; in the bottom example, only the active Modal exists in the tree.
Migration windows by component category
After overlays came basic controls, forms, and display components. They all followed the exact same workflow: merge the new component into base-ui, switch product call sites over, and finally ban the legacy import via ESLint. Each bar below runs from when the new component merged to when the legacy import was banned:
A stark dividing line is visible around August. Before August, taking a component category from initial merge to banning legacy imports took weeks or months: Modal and Select took nearly four months, and form controls took 36 days. After August, Drawer took 5 days, Alert 6 days, Skeleton 3 days, DraggablePanel and Tree 2 days each, while ActionIcon, Avatar, Tag, and Text took just 1 day combined. The migration process hadn't changed—what changed was the models. Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 on June 9 and Claude Opus 5 on July 24. To me, Opus 5 felt exceptionally strong at front-end tasks, and at half the price of Fable 5, it cost about the same as Opus 4.8. By August, commits in lobe-chat switched from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, and Fable 5 usage was rising too. The bars for Tabs and Segmented are also very short, but only because the initial preset banned five components all at once on June 26—not because they migrated faster.
Components like DropdownMenu, Tooltip, and Popover were replaced in place at the root entry point without legacy versions to ban, so they aren't shown in the chart. Commits for each component:
Modal
,
Menu
,
Tooltip
,
Button
,
Form controls
,
Drawer
,
Alert
,
ActionIcon and three others
,
Skeleton
,
DraggablePanel
, and
Tree
.
Each new component had to be a drop-in replacement, matching the old version in both API and visuals so switching only meant changing import paths. In lobe-ui#621, Tag's color resolution was ported straight from the old implementation: 13 preset colors, 5 system colors, and and all four variants (solid, filled, outlined, borderless) across three sizes had to match. Avatar replaced antd Avatar with native
img
, keeping the fallback on load failure and the +N counter for AvatarGroup. After Drawer merged, a separate
commit
followed to align its surface, edges, and drop shadows with antd Drawer.
The ban rules lived in lobe-ui's built-in ESLint preset, inherited directly by product projects. The
initial preset
on June 26 deprecated and banned imports of five antd-based wrappers: Button, Modal, Segmented, Select, and Tabs. When that first version went live, product code still had numerous legacy calls, which were temporarily grandfathered via an allowlist (detailed in the next section). From that point on, rules for each component category were added to the preset only after downstream projects had cleared all legacy imports. The PR description in
lobe-ui#610
was blunt: downstream migrations had removed legacy imports for these components, and this PR turned the migration boundary into an enforceable lint rule. That way, new code couldn't introduce old patterns, and legacy usage could only ever go down.
On the product side: freeze new usage, then clear legacy code category by category
Each time lobe-ui finished migrating a component category, lobe-chat had to update corresponding call sites. The chart below shows the number of files directly importing antd in lobe-chat, sampled biweekly:
Until mid-June, this line kept rising—climbing from 338 in mid-February to 485 on June 15. While legacy calls were being replaced, new features continued using antd. By then, the team had already delegated most product coding to AI, and component precedence had long been codified into
AGENTS.md
and react skills:
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
Any component available in it had to be imported from it, with same-named components at the root entry point off-limits, leaving antd strictly as a fallback when neither had it. Agents routinely ignored this. Because training data and hundreds of existing files demonstrated antd patterns, PRs for new features kept using legacy components even after lobe-ui published replacements. To an agent, docs are merely suggestions. The only way to stop them was to make violations break the build: ESLint fails directly, and lint-staged runs the same checks in pre-commit hooks to block the commit.
That was precisely what
lobehub#16334
did on June 26: it adopted lobe-ui's ESLint preset, banning the five legacy wrappers (Button, Modal, Segmented, Select, Tabs) as well as antd-style's
createStyles
; existing call sites (354 in total) were added to
eslint-suppressions.json
for temporary exemption, while any new violations failed immediately. Afterward, whenever a batch was migrated, we ran
eslint --prune-suppressions
, ensuring the allowlist only ever shrank.
Legacy code was cleared category by category: each PR targeted only one component category, but covered the entire repository. The count dropped slowly over the summer, followed by a steep drop in early October.
lobehub#20247
touched 285 files in one go, swapping out all remaining instances of Table, DatePicker, Menu, List, Input variants, and more, eliminating 163 files with direct antd imports. The PR included before-and-after screenshots compared against canary for verification, and five component library issues caught along the way were patched in
lobe-ui#675
. Next,
lobehub#20317
migrated forms, removing another 63 files;
lobehub#20408
updated menu item types to lobe-ui's, shedding 21 files; finally,
lobehub#20503
cleaned up the remainder. The two files still remaining on November 1 in the chart are test fixtures for alint.
Behavioral discrepancies are harder to catch than visual differences
Visual differences are easy to spot by comparing screenshots side by side, but behavioral discrepancies usually don't surface until a user saves data. After lobehub#20317 migrated forms to base-ui, the values returned on submit differed between the two:
antd Form
base-ui Form
Returned on submit
Values of currently mounted
Form.Item
fields only
Entire form store
Conditionally hidden fields
Discarded
Submitted together
initialValues
extra keys
Discarded
Submitted together
Fields that used to be quietly dropped were now persisted together. Switching a plugin's authentication from bearer to none left the old token behind. Similarly, switching transport from HTTP to stdio kept the old URL, causing later re-installations to fetch manifests from that stale address and overwrite existing settings.
lobehub#20644
added a
pruneHiddenFields
step before saving to prune fields that don't belong to the active type.
The compatibility layer itself can introduce bugs. The
ImperativeModal
wrapper, created for a smooth migration, unmounted its content in the very same commit that
open
became
false
, while base-ui's panel still had a 120ms exit animation—so closing the Skill Store details modal caused the content to collapse prematurely. Instead of patching the wrapper,
lobehub#17941
replaced all 11 call sites with imperative
createModal
Content lives inside a ModalHost and is only unmounted after the exit animation finishes.
Bumping the ecosystem libraries along with lobe-ui's majors
As we wrapped up the app-level cleanup, the intermediate ecosystem tier had to come along. Beyond lobe-ui, lobe-chat depends on icons, editor, charts, tts, and fluent-emoji—most of which declare lobe-ui as a peer dependency:
Whenever lobe-ui bumped a major version, the ecosystem layer broke: downstream packages lost exports they still needed, or peer versions fell out of sync. As a result, we always released them all together:
lobe-ui
Release date
icons
editor
charts
fluent-emoji
v3 (upgraded to antd v6)
2025-12-20
v3
v2
v3
v4 (static styles)
2025-12-24
v4
v3
v4
v5 (base-ui subpackage)
2026-03-02
v5
v4
v5
unchanged
v6 (dropped antd)
2026-10-15
v6
v5
v6
v5
v6 was by far the biggest set of changes, split into a stacked sequence of PRs:
lobe-ui#699
removed the antd components and
ThemeProvider
;
lobe-ui#700
dropped the antd, antd-style, and rc-* dependencies; and
lobe-ui#702
merged
src/base-ui
completely empty.
@lobehub/ui/base-ui
back into the root directory, getting rid of the base-ui subpath. With the coexistence phase over, we tore down that v5 scaffolding and exported the new components straight from the root entry. In early October, the downstream libraries first ported their own component usage over to base-ui (
lobe-editor#222
and
lobe-charts#32
), before each bumped to lobe-ui 6 and stripped out antd.
This cascade of changes couldn't be released and verified piecemeal. Instead, we tested across repos using pkg.pr.new preview packages: PRs for lobe-ui and the five downstream libraries each published preview packages, and
lobehub#20503
pointed all dependencies to those preview URLs. We compared lobe-chat against production page by page to ensure zero visual regressions before officially publishing in dependency order and and then switched back to real version numbers. PR #20503 alone updated imports across 2,728 files, purged antd from 24 workspace packages, and finally left
pnpm ls -r antd
with nothing to show.
Moving styles from runtime generation to build-time compilation
Dropping antd took care of components, but styles were still being generated at runtime. lobe-ui wrote its component styles in antd-style, built on Emotion: on page load, JavaScript generated CSS on the fly and inserted it into the page. The initial optimization pass replaced dynamic hooks with
createStaticStyles
, ensuring components no longer recomputed styles on every re-render. Yet the insertion step remained. In September,
lobehub#19066
pre-computed purely static calls at build time, slashing the time spent on styles during cold home page loads from ~56ms to ~28ms. The remaining ~14ms came from
insertRule
itself—an unavoidable cost as long as emotion was in the loop.
To eliminate this remaining overhead, styles needed to compile down to plain CSS files at build time. I chose StyleX, which splits styles into deduplicated atomic classes during compilation. The underlying mechanics—and how I migrated 10,000 lines of CSS to StyleX on another project—are covered in
"From Pure CSS to StyleX: Migrating 10,000 Lines of CSS with AI"
. For lobe-ui 6,
lobe-ui#701
piloted the approach on six components: Button, Divider, Spin, Switch, Tag, and Tooltip. Then
lobe-ui#705
migrated the remaining 89 modules in one go, freeing all 95 component modules from their emotion dependency. Markup not directly rendered by lobe-ui—such as Markdown, KaTeX, and code syntax highlighting—was styled with plain CSS in
@layer lobe-ui
.
Migrating 89 modules in a single pass succeeded thanks to per-element visual regression testing: we captured 500 demos in the documentation site across both light and dark themes while comparing computed styles for every element. Out of 1,000 runs, 891 matched completely. The remaining runs differed only because of animation timing, image loading, Mermaid layout jitter, or subpixel antialiasing differences. We also installed the packaged bundle into lobe-chat and ran the same comparison across 45 routes and 5 open menus.
Here are median cold-start metrics for the authenticated home page in lobe-chat, with CPU throttled 4x and each build tested across 8 runs. Both builds had already shed antd; the only difference was whether styles were generated at runtime via emotion or compiled ahead of time via StyleX:
Runtime overhead dropped across the board: document CSS rules fell from 5,817 to 4,429, blocking time decreased by 9%, and style recalculations dropped by 8%. The downside was First Contentful Paint: 4G FCP climbed from 440ms to 594ms because lobe-ui's
style.css
bundled styles for all 95 components, weighing in at 179KB uncompressed. In lobe-chat, it ended up in the single render-blocking stylesheet, pushing initial blocking CSS from 20.2KB to 45.5KB (gzipped). On November 2,
lobe-ui#776
introduced the fix: per-component stylesheets, so applications only pull in what they use. In a benchmark app using 30 components, per-component loading yielded 45.9KB, compared to 59.5KB for the full
style.css
bundle. lobe-chat is currently still running on the monolithic
style.css
and hasn't made the switch yet.
What antd was doing behind the scenes
Once antd and emotion were completely removed from the dependency tree, hidden assumptions began surfacing. Beyond providing components, antd silently did plenty of heavy lifting for the entire page: setting root fonts and sizes, providing baseline icon layout, and supplying a global reset. None of this was ever stated in application code—it only became visible after antd was removed:
Symptom
Cause
Fix
Text without a font size falls back to a 16px system font
antd's
App
previously set the font family, font size, line height, and color for everything underneath
theme.css
puts them back in the lowest cascade layer,
@layer lobe-base
, leaving
html
alone so rem values don't change; see
lobe-ui#703
Icons sit 2–3px higher than the text beside them
.anticon
's
inline-flex
and
vertical-align
were previously provided by antd styles
Icon now supplies these baseline layout rules itself; see
lobe-ui#705
List rows stop inheriting the app's font settings
During migration, expanding the
font: inherit
shorthand into longhand lost
font-feature-settings
along with other properties only reset by the shorthand
Fixed by reverting to
font: inherit
; see also lobe-ui#705
ScrollShadow
stops hiding scrollbars
Because component styles moved into
@layer lobe-ui
, the app's unlayered
* { scrollbar-width: thin }
rule took higher priority
Remove the duplicate global rule from the app, or place it below
lobe-ui
in the cascade
The last two issues both trace back to CSS cascade layers. Placing component styles into
@layer
, the layer hierarchy (from lowest to highest) looked like this:
Unlayered styles always beat layered styles, regardless of selector specificity. That makes overriding component styles easy, but, an offhand global rule in application code can also quietly stomp over components.
The icon vertical misalignment was the trickiest to catch. The visual regression tool mentioned in lobe-ui#705 used the v6 preview as its baseline. But
.anticon
styles had vanished earlier when
lobe-ui#699
stripped antd, so the regression was already baked into the baseline, leaving the diff completely empty. We eventually caught it with the naked eye in the Tree component. Once we added a visual comparison against an antd-era lobe-chat build, vertical alignment across 73 icons and text elements snapped into place on the home page, appearance settings, and community page—where the pre-fix preview had matched only 3. A visual regression baseline must be the last version users actually saw, not the previous commit.
Conversely, bugs in the old implementation could also sneak into the baseline. emotion's
cx
merges multiple class names into one, which prevented the
& + &
divider rule in lobe-chat's workspace empty state from matching any element. After the move to StyleX, it kicked in for the first time, and the comparison tool flagged it as a diff. We kept this change as intended behavior.
How much lighter is a Button after dropping antd?
Because application code in the main lobe-chat bundle was also evolving over the year, comparing it before and after wouldn't isolate what changed in the component library itself. Instead, I spun up a clean Vite project rendering a single Button, building it with v5 (5.64.4, with the antd Button) and v6 (6.15.0). Both setups included only what was strictly necessary for rendering: v5 wrapped the button in
ThemeProvider
, while v6 imported
theme.css
alongside the Button stylesheet, plus a
MotionProvider
.
Excluding React, Button-related JS dropped from ~130KB to ~32KB. The bulk of v5 came from antd and its rc-component dependencies, totaling around 287KB uncompressed; v6's 32KB mostly belongs to the motion animation library, with lobe-ui itself accounting for just ~9KB uncompressed. The tradeoff is that v6 introduces a static CSS file measuring 22.6KB gzipped, of which 16.5KB is "}
theme.css
design tokens, shared across all components; v5 shipped no CSS files because JavaScript generated styles at runtime, shared across all components and generated styles at runtime with JS.
During benchmarking, we also uncovered an issue: importing from the root entry
import { Button } from '@lobehub/ui'
, both versions pulled in around 450KB of unminified —or roughly 141KB gzipped KaTeX and Markdown parsing code that had nothing to do with Button. The figures above already exclude this overhead. In v6, importing from the
es/Button
subpath avoids pulling it in entirely, whereas v5 only exported the root entry, leaving no way around it. The reason was that the root entry re-exported
@lobehub/streamdown
's
rehypeStreamAnimated
, but streamdown's package.json didn't declare
sideEffects
, and the module top level contained impure
memo()
calls and
displayName
assignments. Because bundlers couldn't prove they were side-effect-free, they had to keep the entire Markdown rendering stack. The fix was shipped in
lobehub/streamdown#7
in version 1.4.5, simply adding to package.json:
"sideEffects": false
. lobe-ui 6's dependency range automatically picks up this new release. After a clean reinstall, importing from the root entry matches the subpath import at 92.4KB.
Beyond bundle size, we also eliminated the leftover styling overhead from antd. The share, workbench, and auth SSR apps previously had to extract antd's static CSS separately;
lobehub#20503
deleted that entire pipeline. We also removed the
antdOverride
global stylesheet that existed solely to override antd defaults, while
lobehub#21046
purged the application CSS rules written for
.ant-*
classes, which no longer match any elements once antd was removed.
Next step: can we migrate Application Code to StyleX in One Go?
With the component library migrated, styling in application code was still using the legacy styling approach: using
createStaticStyles
at the top of a file to write CSS in template strings, which Emotion then injected into the page at runtime. On canary, 1,112 files still follow this pattern, while around 350 have been converted to StyleX. On October 20,
lobehub#21042
paved the way for writing StyleX in application code, allowing direct imports of lobe-ui design tokens. Below is a file from the homepage sidebar notifications list, shown before and after the rewrite in
lobehub#21446
:
Before:
createStaticStyles
CodeBlock Loading...
After: StyleX
CodeBlock Loading...
Rewriting a single file isn't hard; the hard part is proving it looks identical afterward. Notice the extra property on the right:
backgroundImage: 'none'
on the right: the original
background
is a shorthand property that also resets the background image. StyleX discourages shorthand properties, which means writing only
backgroundColor
drops that reset. The
font: inherit
pitfall in the earlier table stems from the exact same issue. Visual differences like this rarely show up in screenshots, and comparing over a thousand files by eye is painfully slow and error-prone. Beyond writing a migrator, we needed an automated tool to confirm styles stayed identical before and after the rewrite and catch pitfalls like the ones above before and after.
Our initial plan was to compare computed styles rather than screenshots: checking browser-computed styles before and after across themes, breakpoints, and hover or focus states for every styled element. Taking HomeSidebar (
lobehub#21446
) and ChatInput (
lobehub#21452
), it caught an actual regression:
Params/Controls.tsx
had its
font: inherit
expanded into longhands, causing the button to lose its
font-feature-settings
. The exact trap we stumbled into in the component library resurfaced during the app migration—except this time the tool caught it first.
Before trusting the tool when it reported "equivalent," we had to prove the tool itself was trustworthy. That verification baseline required three things: tell noise from real differences by remaining completely stable when comparing a version against itself; catch actual regressions by flagging 100% of intentionally injected changes; and know its limits by deferring anything synthetic rendering can't cover to human review, storing those sign-offs with the source code and invalidating them whenever the code changes.
Once the baseline was locked in, we re-ran all 16 migration PRs summarized in
lobehub#22041
. The results fell into three buckets: proven equivalent and passed immediately, divergent and sent back for fixes, or unprovable and escalated for human review.
To save reviewers from digging through logs, I built a local reporting UI. The overview lists results by file and condition, letting you click into any element to inspect evidence and see a side-by-side live comparison. Meanwhile, the sign-off page groups items by root cause for batch approval.
Report overview: one row per file, one column per condition. ✓ indicates equivalent; numbers show counts of differing elements.
Sign-off view: grouped by reason, with side-by-side renders comparing before and after under the same condition
Summary
Between December 2025 and October 2026, lobe-ui evolved from v3 to v6, direct antd imports in lobe-chat dropped from a peak of 485 files to zero, and the JS footprint for a single Button shrank from around 130KB to roughly 32KB (gzipped). Looking back, once AI and codemods made rewriting code cheap, the real bottlenecks came down to two challenges: creating coexistence mechanisms and guardrails so shipping never stopped while legacy patterns continuously shrank, and automatically proving with tooling that behavior and styles hadn't regressed. A few key practices from this year transfer well to other projects:
Let new and legacy components coexist in the same package, migrating component by component.
v5's
base-ui
subpath spared application code from an all-or-nothing rewrite, allowing us to tear down that scaffolding in v6.
Migrate the highest-overhead, most interconnected layer first.
Overlays share positioning and z-index logic. Declarative modals stay mounted all the time, whereas an imperative approach only incurs overhead when a modal actually opens.
Make new components drop-in replacements.
Match both the API and visual appearance of legacy components so app code only changes import paths, porting over quirks like Tag's color resolution verbatim.
Lock down migrated categories with lint rules, grandfathering existing usage via allowlists.
AGENTS.md
and skills couldn't prevent AI agents from mimicking legacy antd patterns found in existing files. Import counts only began to steadily decline once we added lint rules and commit hooks on June 26.
Verify equivalence via computed styles, using the version users actually see as the baseline.
.anticon
positioning drift and
font: inherit
attribute loss both slipped past screenshot diffs and "compare against previous version" checks.
Isolate variables when measuring gains.
Instead of benchmarking entire production bundles, spin up a dedicated project rendering only a single Button—which also uncovered our root entry tree-shaking bug.

items.target: October’s Critical CVEs, Two Weeks On
items.text: hacktron-blog published: October’s Critical CVEs, Two Weeks On
items.title: October’s Critical CVEs, Two Weeks On
items.content:
Between 16 and 23 October, five major security incidents went public in a single week: two remote code execution bugs in PHP, a memory corruption bug in Google’s Brotli decoder, a chain of four bugs in Plex Media Server, a CVSS 10.0 bug in GitLab, and eight compromised certificate authority keys at eMudhra.
Now that the month is over, here’s what happened next.
At a glance
Issue
Patch / containment
Exploitation
PHP2Shell (
CVE-2026-109618
,
CVE-2026-109619
)
21 Oct
Attempt seen 17 Oct, before disclosure; CISA-listed 26 Oct; 24 PAN-OS firewalls rooted (Dream Research)
HTTP2Shell / Node2Shell (
CVE-2026-111497
)
21 Oct
CISA-listed as exploited 27 Oct; public details of compromises limited. ELLIO’s documented attempt failed in lab replays
Plex2Shell (four CVEs)
Early Aug
CISA-listed 20 Oct; active exploitation confirmed by Plex: crypto miners, proxy malware
GitLab (
CVE-2026-110264
)
21 Oct
No public exploitation reported
GitLab (
CVE-2026-97229
, earlier flaw)
12 Oct
Exploitation attempts detected by GitLab; Alpine Linux targeted 20–21 Oct; CISA cites ongoing attacks
eMudhra CA keys
17 Oct (blocked)
No malicious use confirmed
PHP2Shell
PHP fixed both bugs on 21 October, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
PHP2Shell: Critical PHP RCE (
CVE-2026-109618,
CVE-2026-109619)
covers who is affected and how to check.
PHP2Shell is being exploited.
Amazon Threat Intelligence
recorded an exploitation attempt in its MadPot honeypots on 17 October, four days before public disclosure, and says it’s unclear how the actor got the exploit details that early. After disclosure, AWS reports broad exploitation attempts in the wild. CISA added both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 26 October.
Palo Alto Networks’ advisory
now says active exploitation has been observed against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. On 26 October,
Dream Research reported a campaign
that chained PHP2Shell with Fragnesia (
CVE-2026-46300
), a Linux kernel privilege-escalation bug, and rooted 24 PAN-OS firewalls in the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, plus an internal management server. Two of the firewalls belonged to a US government-affiliated organisation. On 29 October,
Unit 42 said
it had independently verified the attacker’s tooling and the reported results. Dream Research found signs of AI-assisted tooling on the attacker’s infrastructure, but says it has no direct evidence AI wrote the exploit.
The attempts started before the fix:
Attack activity
Fix or response
PHP2Shell is a blind remote memory corruption bug. A proof of concept built for one target rarely works on the next one, because memory layout depends on the PHP build, the extensions loaded, and the application in front of it. Code execution needs an exploit tuned to each target.
That doesn’t make the bug overhyped. Attempts are widespread; confirmed successful compromises are much rarer.
Wiz says
it hasn’t seen a successful end-to-end PHP2Shell exploit in its own telemetry.
We measured how long that adaptation takes
: frontier models ported the exploit to a new target in hours, while the open models we tested didn’t get there. That gap is likely to narrow.
A separate PHP issue is still open. On 23 October,
PHP published an advisory
for
CVE-2026-115560
, another possible remote code execution path through session upload progress. It needs an unusual configuration: a non-default session serializer in server settings that the application switches back at runtime with
ini_set()
before
session_start()
. The 21 October releases don’t fix it, and no fix release is out yet. PHP’s mitigation for affected configurations is to set
session.upload_progress.enabled=0
at the server level. No exploitation has been reported.
The attacks a vendor has confirmed so far are against firewall management interfaces. Most people don’t think of their firewall as a PHP server, but its management interface runs PHP under the hood.
HTTP2Shell / Node2Shell (Brotli)
The fixes shipped on 21 October, in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1, and 1.0.10, and in Node.js 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4. Fixes are still landing in software that bundles its own copy of Brotli. Linux distributions may backport the fix under older-looking version numbers, so check your distro’s security tracker rather than the version string alone.
CISA added
CVE-2026-111497
to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 27 October, citing evidence of active exploitation. Public details of successful compromises remain limited.
On 26 October, threat-intelligence firm
ELLIO documented an exploitation attempt
involving a Brotli-compressed request targeting Node.js 24.22.0 on x86-64. When ELLIO replayed the attacker’s chain in its lab, the final stage failed in all 50 attempts. The same source IP had been associated with PHP2Shell activity in OffSeq’s honeypots the week before.
The bug isn’t limited to Node.js. On 25 October,
Microsoft shipped out-of-band .NET updates
(8.0.33, 9.0.22, and 10.0.14) for the same flaw in .NET’s use of Brotli; request and automatic response decompression are off by default, and self-contained apps and containers carry their own runtime, so they need rebuilding. On 28 October,
AWS published a bulletin
saying its .NET and Node.js Lambda runtimes are affected, along with App Runner, CodeBuild curated images, and other services. AWS has updated the Lambda container base images, so rebuild and redeploy those functions. Node.js functions deployed as ZIP files now run on Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.2, or 26.13.0. To confirm a function has the update, find its runtime version in the
INIT_START
line of its logs and compare it with the patched Node.js and .NET versions in the bulletin. AWS recommends moving functions on Manual or Function Update mode to Auto.
Where the bug has turned up, with upstream fixed versions and what to do as of 3 November:
Component
Fixed in
What to do
Brotli library
1.0.10, 1.1.1, 1.2.1
Update Brotli wherever bundled; rebuild images
Node.js
22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1
Upgrade, then restart processes
.NET
8.0.33, 9.0.22, 10.0.14
Update, rebuild self-contained apps
Python Brotli / brotlicffi
1.2.1 / 1.2.1.0
Upgrade the package
Bun
1.4.4
Upgrade
AWS Lambda (Node.js, .NET)
Images and ZIP runtimes patched
Rebuild containers; check runtime version
AWS App Runner
26 Oct
Update pinned runtime; redeploy
Brotli is hard to fingerprint from the outside. A server doesn’t announce which decoder it uses, and the bug only matters if something decodes attacker-controlled Brotli data: request bodies, or responses fetched from a server the attacker controls.
We covered the bug and the exploit path in more detail in
Node2Shell: Brotli Decoder RCE in Node.js (
CVE-2026-111497)
.
Plex2Shell
Plex fixed the issue in version 1.43.3.10861, released in early August.
Attackers began exploiting it about a day after the 16 October write-up.
A researcher’s honeypot recorded attacks
on 17 October that installed an XMRig-based crypto miner and proxy software, and Plex has confirmed active exploitation. No one has published a count of compromised servers. CISA added all four CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 20 October.
This is the only one of the five where the fix was out for more than two months before the attacks. Plex Media Server mostly runs on home and small-office machines, often exposed for remote streaming, and often not updated until something breaks.
GitLab (
CVE-2026-110264
)
GitLab fixed this flaw on 21 October, in 19.5.1, 19.4.3, and 19.3.6, with backports to four older branches. GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated were patched before disclosure.
No public exploitation has been reported for this flaw. The bug was in the Ruby regular expression engine GitLab ships, not in GitLab’s own code.
An earlier GitLab flaw in the same family is under attack.
GitLab says it has detected exploitation attempts
against
CVE-2026-97229
, fixed on 12 October, and has published detection rules. Shadowserver tracks nearly 2,800 internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, though it hasn’t said how many are patched.
The best-documented case is
Alpine Linux
, whose GitLab instance was targeted on 20 and 21 October. Alpine found no evidence the attacker succeeded but couldn’t rule it out, so it rebuilt the instance, reset all passwords and replaced GitLab’s secret keys. Alpine had two patching misses. Before the attack, it upgraded to GitLab 19.3.4 instead of the patched 19.3.5 by mistake. Then its upgrade to 19.3.6 on 22 October, after the attempts, still didn’t close the path: the fix is a patch to Ruby that GitLab only applies in its official packages, and Alpine’s image used standard Ruby.
The sequence, from Alpine’s 28 October incident report and CISA:
Attack activity
Missed fix
Fix or response
If you self-host GitLab and haven’t upgraded, do it now. A successful exploit could expose repositories and CI/CD secrets accessible to the GitLab service account.
eMudhra
Chrome blocked the eight affected keys within two hours of the 17 October report, and other browsers and runtimes followed. Chrome stopped trusting the affected eMudhra root certificate on 27 October.
No public exploitation has been reported.
Google says
no website certificates from the affected intermediates had appeared in Certificate Transparency logs before the block, and
eMudhra says
it isn’t aware of any evidence the weak keys were recovered or exploited before disclosure. eMudhra’s board decided on 22 October to leave the global TLS certificate business.
If you have certificates chained to the eMudhra root, they need replacing with another CA.
Is there a pattern?
The PHP2Shell attacks a vendor has confirmed are on firewall appliances. Plex2Shell’s are self-hosted media servers with a fix from two months prior. ELLIO’s publicly documented Brotli exploit attempt was built for a specific Node.js build. In each case, the vulnerable code sits inside something people don’t think of as theirs to patch, such as a vendor’s appliance, a home media server, a bundled runtime, or a container base image.
Those are also the copies a version scan tends to miss. Brotli is compiled into runtimes and libraries that don’t list it as a dependency. GitLab’s fixes are in the Ruby it ships, which is why Alpine’s upgraded instance stayed vulnerable. And as of 28 October,
the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre
was tracking 757 products for PHP2Shell, with 218 confirmed vulnerable, 144 fixed, 354 still under investigation, 40 not affected, and one unassessed.
A patch existing doesn’t mean systems are patched.
Wiz’s telemetry
shows the number of internet-exposed machines vulnerable to PHP2Shell fell about 67% in the first week, but nearly half of the organisations originally affected were still vulnerable a week after disclosure. The remaining risk is in the copies you may not have realised you need to update. Check what’s actually running across your environment, and look for signs of exploitation that may have happened before you patched.
Sources
CISA: critical vulnerabilities in PHP require immediate patching
AWS: PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure
Palo Alto Networks advisory:
CVE-2026-109618
Unit 42 threat brief:
CVE-2026-109618 and
CVE-2026-109619
OffSeq: PHP2Shell, the first 48 hours
ELLIO: Node2Shell analysis
SecurityAffairs on Plex2Shell
eMudhra statement
Dream Research: chained PHP2Shell exploit roots 25 servers
Alpine Linux: GitLab security incident (
CVE-2026-97229)
THN: CISA adds actively exploited GitLab RCE to KEV
BleepingComputer: hackers now exploiting max severity GitLab flaw
Wiz: PHP2Shell exploitation attempts and remediation trends
NCSC-NL: PHP2Shell operational information
Tenable: PHP2Shell one week later
Check Point on HTTP2Shell
Node.js October 2026 security releases
Bun advisory: bundled Brotli decoder (
CVE-2026-111497)
GitHub advisory: Brotli decoder in the PyPI Brotli package
Microsoft: .NET October 2026 out-of-band security updates
AWS security bulletin 2026-155-AWS: Brotli
PHP
CVE-2026-115560 advisory
Secure.com on Plex2Shell
GitLab patch release 19.5.1
Google on eMudhra
THN: eMudhra to exit global SSL/TLS business
